3 Fri Sept 11 - Models and quantities 3.1 Models Almost every biological theory or hypothesis is a model of how nature works. The model can be written in mathematical notation for clarity. For example, \[ P_{corn} = \alpha + \beta_{Psoil} P_{soil} + \epsilon \] describes our hypothesis that phosphorus levels in the soil determine phosphorous levels in corn. This equation comprises of symbols, and unless we define these symbols the equation is meaningless. \(P_{corn}\) and \(P_{soil}\) are symbols that correspond to data (or measured quantities, see below). \(\alpha\), \(\beta_{Psoil}\), and \(\epsilon\) are symbols that we need to describe our model, i.e., our hypothesis of how the phosphorous in the soil is related to the phosphorus in the soil. If \(P_{corn}\) and \(P_{soil}\) are measured quantities on the ratio scale and if we assume that the differences between the model-predicted values and the data, \(\epsilon\), are independent and normally distributed (with equal variance), then the name of this model is a linear regression (with one predictor variable). Our model describes the signal and the noise. Is there evidence for the signal, or are we just describing the noise? 3.2 Models and data We use data to separate models that are more likely correct from ones that are less likely correct. We should consider what kind of data do we need? Our population is the set of all objects that we wish to apply our conclusions to. The data we collect are samples from the population. Samples need to be representative of the population. This is best done by choosing them randomly. To determine if a model (our hypothesis) is supported by the data, we need to assess model fit, if the assumptions of the model are met, and the values of estimated parameters. For example, if \(\hat{\beta}_{Psoil} = 0\), where \(\hat{\beta}_{Psoil}\) is the estimated slope for the relationship between \(P_{corn}\) and \(P_{soil}\) for our data, then this says there is no relationship between the phosphorous in the soil and in the corn. There are different approaches to assessing if a model fits well and if a model is better than it’s competitors. You may already have heard of hypothesis testing, confidence intervals, and Bayesian statistics. Different approaches have strengths and weakness and you should understand what each approach involves. We can find a ‘best’ model from a model set, but not a ‘correct’ model. There can be multiple ways to correctly complete the statistics for your problem, and… … there are some choices that are wrong. Being wrong could be due to a mismatch between: (a) the biological question and the sampling design - you can’t link the pattern in the data to the biological model; (b) your statistical model and the biological situation - you get a clear view from the analysis, but it doesn’t answer your question; (c) your statistical model and the sampling or experimental design - you do not have confidence in your estimates; and (d) the statistical model and your data - conclusions are unrealiable if assumptions of the statistical test are not met. 3.3 Data are measured quantities To clearly write our model we need to establish some best standards for reporting and describing our data. Data are measured quantities. Measured quantities should have a name, symbol, a set of scaled numbers, units, and a procedural statement. Types of measured quantities are: nominal, ordinal, interval, and ratio. You should know what type your data is (for each variable). Which type of data you are using to test your biological hypotheses guides how you complete your statistical test. Nominal. Outcome of measurement is “yes” or “no” also coded as 0 or 1. Ordinal. Outcome is ranking: 1st, 2nd, 3rd, etc. There is no information about magnitude of difference from one rank to next. Interval. The distance between measurements is known, but zero is an arbitrary point. Addition and subtraction are valid. Multiplication and division are not. Example of compass direction. Direction is relative to an arbitrary point. Other examples are Dates (2 January, Julian day 180). Ratio. Distance between measurements is known, zero point is absolute, not arbitrary. An example is degrees Kelvin. There is no heat content at 0\(^\circ\)K In contrast, 0\(^\circ\)C does not mean “no temperature.” Molecular motion (heat) is still present. So 0\(^\circ\)C is interval. This categorization of types of measured quantities is based on Dr. Schneider’s past lectures. The types of variables (discrete or continuous, where Quinn and Keough use the term variables as Dr. Schneider uses measured quantities) are described by Quinn and Keough and summarized here. The Quinn and Keough description has more relevance to choice of statistical test, and I will use that framework for future teaching of the course. Completing assignment 1 will help you understand what measured quantities are. This will help you understand the expectations for how should discuss your data in scientific writing and will prepare you for writing your statistical tests as equations, which allows you to communicate your biological hypotheses clearly. 3.4 Readings This lecture is based on the following readings: Ch1: Introduction by Quinn and Keough. 4 Mon Sept 14 - Equations, units, and notation 4.1 Ratio scale units You can rescale, i.e., grams to kilograms. Suppose, we estimated that \(\hat{\beta} = 2\) and \(\hat{\alpha} = 0\) for a regression \(y = \hat{\alpha} + \hat{\beta} x\). If we consider a specific value of \(x_1 = 1\), what is the value of \(y_1\) predicted by the best fit line? 4.2 Equations Units must balance across an equals (homogeneity of units). In the previous example, if the units of \(y\) are grams and the units of \(x\) are parts per million (ppm), what are the units of each of \(\hat{\alpha}\) and \(\hat{\beta}\)? The hypothesis and assumptions for common statistical tests should be written as equations. The symbols should have biological interpretations and units. Estimated coefficients and quantities, i.e., slopes, coefficients, and standard deviations have units and should be presented as such. 4.3 Data equations A data equation: data = model + residual. Statistical tests often assume the residual follows a probability distribution. In symbols: \(y = E(H) + \epsilon\), where \(y\) are the data and \(\epsilon\) are the residuals. Here \(E(H)\) is your model, or what you expect under your hypothesis. You might expect a particular value, i.e., \(E(H) = 0.3\) or you might expect a linear relationship with a predictor variable, i.e., \(E(H) = \alpha + \beta x\). Statistical models have explanatory (or predictor) variables and response variables. Practice calculating the residual for set of data points practice calculating the residual and the residual sum of squares (see the heterozygousity example in Example 5.2 Fruit fly heterozygosity in Ch 5 Data equations). How is bias calculated? Draw an illustration of positive and negative bias. For a model with no predictor variable (no consideration of elevation) what is the best fit estimate of heterozygosity from the sample? How was this estimate calculated? What were the two criteria to define ‘best fit’? Some questions we will re-visit in future classes: What is the likelihood and how is it calculated? What is the likelihood ratio? What are degrees of freedom? 4.4 Some common notations \(E(H)\) denotes the expected value. \(\hat{\beta}\) denotes an estimated value of \(\beta\). \(X\) denotes a realization of a random variable, where the random variable may follow a probability distribution such as \(P(X=x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi \sigma^2}}e^{-(x-\mu)^2/2\sigma^2}\). \(X \sim P(X=x)\) means ‘X is distributed as P(X=x)’. Note that it is not correct to say \(X\) is equal to \(P(X=x)\) is \(X\) is a realization from a probability distribution. \(L(\beta|X)\) is the likelihood of a parameter value, \(\beta\), given the data, \(X\). 4.5 Readings Ch2.5: Ratio scale units Ch4: Equations Ch5: Data equations

5 Wed Sept 16 - Samples and populations 5.1 Samples and populations Populations are all possible units and their associated observations of interest. Samples are a collection of observations from a population. The number of units in the sample is the sample size. Variables, or measured quantities, are the characteristics that we record. Variables can be continuous, taking any value within a range, i.e., weight. Discrete variables can be ordered along the continuous scale (e.g., counts), and in some cases there are so many possibility that discrete variables can be treated essentially as continuous. For example, hypotheses that involve count data, when the values are large, are often tested with the same statistical tests as continuous data. (Based on 2.1 of Quinn and Keough)

See here for the instructions. 6.2 Last 20 minutes: Quiz 1 6.3 Probability and probability distributions Probabilities satisfy Kolmogorov’s properties. Probabilities can be interpreted as the relative frequency of an event, or the ‘degree of belief’ an event will occur. Bayes’ theorem relates to conditional probability \(P(A|B)\), which is the probability an event \(A\) will occur given and event \(B\). Bayes’ theorem is fundamental to Bayesian statistics. The definition of independence is that that the probability of events \(A\) and \(B\) occurring can be calculated by multiplying their probabilities: \(P(A,B) = P(A)P(B)\). We may not be justified in using that formula if \(A\) and \(B\) are not independent. We we say that our statistical method assumes that our residuals are independent, we mean that we can multiply the probabilities associated with each residual to calculate the probability of observing these residuals for all the data, i.e., \(P(\epsilon_1, \dots, \epsilon_n) = \prod_{i=1}^n P(\epsilon_i)\). We will specifically show that we are using this assumption when we take the maximum likelihood approach to deriving the residual sum of squares formula (in a future lecture). 6.3.1 Probability distributions for variables 6.3.1.1 The normal (or Gaussian) distribution The normal distribution arises frequently in statistics. Mathematically, it can be shown that the sum of independent identically distributed random variables are normally distributed, which can be appropriate to model many sources of error. The formula for the normal distribution is, \[f(y) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}e^{-(y-\mu)^2/2\sigma^2}, \] where \(y\) is the independent variable, \(f(y)\) is the probability density for a particular \(y\) value, \(\mu\) is the mean and \(\sigma^2\) is the variance. The standard normal distribution has a mean, \(\mu = 0\), and variance, \(\sigma^2 = 1\). Notationally, we might write the standard normal distribution as \(N(0,1)\) where \(N(\mu,\sigma^2)\) is the normal distribution with a mean of \(\mu\) and variance of \(\sigma^2\). 6.3.1.2 The Binomial distribution The binomial distribution also frequently occurs in statistics. A coin toss is an example of a Bernoulli trial. The formula for the binomial distribution is, \[P(y=k) = \frac{n!}{k!(n-k)!}p^k(1-p)^{p-k} \] where \(k\) is the number of successes for \(n\) Bernoulli trials, each with a probability of success \(p\). This formula can be executed in R with the commands below. Try cutting and pasting the commands into your R console. To understand the arguments of the dbinom() function read the R help file here. k = seq(0,10) binom.probs=data.frame(k=k,P=dbinom(k, 10, 0.5)) binom.probs ## k P ## 1 0 0.0009765625 ## 2 1 0.0097656250 ## 3 2 0.0439453125 ## 4 3 0.1171875000 ## 5 4 0.2050781250 ## 6 5 0.2460937500 ## 7 6 0.2050781250 ## 8 7 0.1171875000 ## 9 8 0.0439453125 ## 10 9 0.0097656250 ## 11 10 0.0009765625 P = select(binom.probs,P) sum(P) ## [1] 1 What is \(p\) and \(n\) for this table? What do you notice about the sum of the probabilities from 0 to \(n\)? Note that select() is a dplyr function to select a column. I have loaded dplyr in the background. I generally recommend dplyr for data manipulation as it makes easy to read code and used by the best coders in professions related to biological statistics. We can also make a nice graph of our binomial distribution with \(p = 0.5\) and \(n=10\). (I also loaded ggplot in the background, which is a widely-used package to make publication quality graphics). ggplot(binom.probs, aes(x = k,y=P)) + geom_bar(fill = "steelblue", stat = "identity")+ scale_x_continuous(breaks = k)+ ggtitle("The Binomial probability distribution with n=10 and p=0.5")+ ylab("P(y=k)") From the graph (and the choice to plot it as a bar plot), we can see that the Binomial distribution describes the probability associated with events that are discrete, i.e., 0, 1, 2, etc. success, and the probability of 2.5 successes, or 11 successes when there are only 10 trials is 0. For discrete variables, the probability distribution is a probability mass function. In contrast, the normal distribution corresponds to continuous variables and this type of probability distribution is called a probability density function. 6.3.1.3 The Poisson distribution The Poisson distribution describes variables representing (typically small) number of occurrences of a particular event, i.e, people kicked by horses. The number of trials is not fixed for the Poisson distribution, and successes (where ‘success’ means a person is kicked by a horse!) occur with a mean rate of \(\mu\). The probability density for the Poisson distribution is, \[P(y=r) = \frac{e^{-\mu}\mu^r}{r!}, \] where this distribution can be understood to represent the probability of \(r\) successes occurring during an observational period. The mean and variance are equal for the Poisson distribution so if count data is over-dispersed we might need to use a negative bionomial distribution instead (which specifies the variance as a parameter) These notes are from Quinn and Keough Ch 2.3.

8 Wed Sept 23 - Frequentist estimation 8.1 Methods of estimation (frequentist estimation) 8.2 Simple parameters and statistics 8.3 Sampling the distribution mean 8.4 Standard error of the sample mean 8.5 Confidence estimates for the population mean 8.6 Standard errors and confidence intervals for other statistics 8.7 Resampling methods for frequentist estimation 8.8 Readings

8 Wed Sept 23 - Frequentist estimation Estimating population parameters from sample data is the goal of statistics. A good estimator should be unbiased. An example of a population parameter is the mean or the standard deviation. You likely already know the formula to calculate the mean, \(\bar{y}\), from a sample of size, \(n\). The formula to calculate the standard deviation is, \[ s = \sqrt{\dfrac{\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \bar{y})^2}{n-1}}. \] Table 2.1 in Quinn and Keough lists other commonly estimated parameters, statistics, and their formulas. Degrees for freedom are the number of observations that are “free to vary” when we estimate a parameter. For example, for a sample of \(n\) observations we have \(n-1\) degrees of freedom to estimate the standard deviation because we use one degree of freedom to estimate the mean. Often the degrees of freedom are \(n-p\) where \(p\) is the number of parameters already estimated. Interval estimates provide a range of values that might include the parameter with a given probability. The confidence interval is a range which we have some confidence that the true value of the parameter might lie in. 8.1 Methods of estimation (frequentist estimation) Ordinary least squares (OLS). The OLS estimator for a parameter minimizes the sum of the squared differences between each sample estimate adn the estimate of the population mean, \(\mu\). Assumes a normal distribution for confidence intervals. Maximum likelihood (ML). The ML estimator for a parameter is the one that maximizes the likelihood of observing the data. 8.2 Simple parameters and statistics Given a sample of observations \((y_1, y_2, \dots, y_n)\) we would usually like to estimate some measures of the data’s central tendency and its spread. The center of the distribution can be measured by the mean or median. The spread (or variability) can be measured by the standard deviation, or the variance, \(s^2\), where the sample variance is calculated as, \[ s^2 = \dfrac{\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \bar{y})^2}{n-1}, \] and where the numerator is the residual sum of squares (RSS), and the denomenator is \(n-1\) (rather than \(n\)) because the \(n-1\) is needed for \(s^2\) to be an unbiased estimate of the population variance. The units of the variance are squared that of the original measurements, while for the standard deviation, \(s = \sqrt{s^2}\), are same units as the original measurements. 8.3 Sampling the distribution mean Having a point estimate of the population mean is only the first step under frequentist estimation, we also need to estimate how variable our estimate might be under repeated sampling from the population. Assume that our sample, \((y_1, y_2, \dots, y_n)\), has come from a normally distributed population. We usually only take one sample from a population, but if we took many samples and plotted the distribution of the sample means the sampling distribution of means ahs the following properties: The probability distribution of means of samples from normal distributions are also normally distributed. As the sample size, \(n\), increases, the probability distributions of means of samples from any distribution will approach a normal distribution. This is a result of the central limit theorem. The expected value, or the mean, of the probability distribution of the sample means is the mean of the population (\(\mu\)) from which the samples where taken. 8.4 Standard error of the sample mean Let’s consider that the sample means have a normal distribution. We can calculate their variance, just as we calculated their mean values. The expected value of the standard deviation (SD) of the sample mean is, \[ \sigma_{\bar{y}} = \frac{\sigma}{n}, \] where \(\sigma\) is the SD of the original population from which the repeated samples were taken. We rarely have many samples from the same population. The SD of the sample means is called the standard error or the mean, and is estimated as, \[ s_{\bar{y}} = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}, \] where \(s\) is the sample estimate of the SD original population (the population the samples are drawn from) adn \(n\) is the sample size. The standard error describes the error in estimating the population mean, \(\mu\), using the sample estimator, \(\bar{y}\). If the standard error, \(s_{\bar{y}}\) is large, then repeated sampling and estimation of the population mean would generate highly variable estimates. 8.5 Confidence estimates for the population mean We can convert any sample mean into its equivalent value from a standard normal distribution as, \[ z = \frac{\bar{y}-\mu}{\sigma_{\bar{y}}}, \] where \(\sigma_{\bar{y}}\) is the standard error (i.e., the SD of the mean). We can then use the quantiles of the standard normal distribution to estimate the range of values that the population mean occurs within withn a given probability, for example: \[ P(\bar{y}-1.96\sigma_{\bar{y}} \leq \mu \leq \bar{y}+1.96\sigma_{\bar{y}}) = 0.95, \] which is an interval estimate for the population mean, \(\mu\), and specifically, given the values above means that there is a 95\(\%\) chance that the sample mean is within the interval, \([\bar{y}-1.96\sigma_{\bar{y}},\bar{y}+1.96\sigma_{\bar{y}}]\). A problem with the fomula above is that we do not know \(\sigma_{\bar{y}}\) which is the population variance, i.e., the true variance, of the distribution of sample means. Generally, we can never know these true population values, we can only try to estimate the true values using estimators. A version of the formula for a 95\(\%\) confidence interval for the population mean, \(\mu\), where we can evaluate all the quantities in the formula is, \[ \bar{y} - t_{0.975, n-1}\dfrac{s}{\sqrt{n}} \quad \leq \quad \mu \quad \leq \quad \bar{y} + t_{0.975, n-1}\dfrac{s}{\sqrt{n}}. \] The sample mean is \(\bar{y} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n y_i\) for a sample with \(n\) observations and where \(s\) is the sample standard deviation (see earlier in these notes for the formula), and the t-statistic (which approaches the standard normal distribution as \(n \to \infty\)) for the quantiles 0.025 and 0.975 with \(n-1\) degrees of freedom can be determined from a look-up table or with the code: n = 100 # number of observations in sample qt(0.975, n-1) ## [1] 1.984217 In the code above \(n\) is specifically set to 100. There is a 95\(\%\) probability that the population mean is between these values. Practice calculating the 95\(\%\) confidence interval for some data. Understand what the estimated quantity means. 8.5.1 Interpretation of confidence intervals for the population mean. We usually do not consider the population mean, \(\mu\), to be a random variable. Rather, we understand the population mean to be fixed value, although we do not know what this value is. The confidence interval is a probability statement about the interval rather than the parameter itself. 8.5.2 Example: Pea lengths For example, consider some data on the github repository, biol-4605-data. I have choosen data describing pea lengths (cm) and then extracted only the control measurements. I am using dplyr commands and I loaded that package in the background. data = read.csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ahurford/biol-4605-data/refs/heads/main/data/pea-length.csv") pea.length = filter(data, treatment=="Control")%>%select(length) pea.length ## length ## 1 65 ## 2 67 ## 3 68 ## 4 70 ## 5 71 ## 6 75 ## 7 76 ## 8 74 ## 9 72 ## 10 68 ## 11 66 The 95\(\%\) confidence interval for these data is: result <- t.test(pea.length, conf.level = 0.95) result$conf.int ## [1] 67.67141 72.69223 ## attr(,"conf.level") ## [1] 0.95 Can you get this same result using the formula? Can you explain what the confidence interval means for this sample of pea lengths? For this pea length example, what is the sample size? Can you calculate the mean and the median? (the answers are below so you can check your answers) mean(pea.length) ## [1] 70.18182 median(pea.length) ## [1] 70 Can you use the formulas to calculate the sample standard deviation, variance, and standard error? (answers below) sd(pea.length) ## [1] 3.736795 var(pea.length) ## [1] 13.96364 std.err ## [1] 1.126686 All of these calculated values have units mm, except for the sample variance which has units mm\(^2\). 8.6 Standard errors and confidence intervals for other statistics The standard error (SE) is the standard deviation (SD) of the probability distribution of a specific statistic, so we can calculate the SE for statistics other than the mean (as described in Sokal and Rohlf, 2012). However, the sample variance is known to follow a \(\chi^2\) distribution and so a 95\(\%\) confidence interval for the population variance is calculated as: \[ \left[\dfrac{s^2(n-1)}{\chi^2_{0.025, n-1}}, \dfrac{s^2(n-1)}{\chi^2_{0.975, n-1}}\right], \] where \(\chi_{\alpha/2, \text{df}}\) is the \(\chi^2\) distribution evaluated at the quantile, \(\alpha/2\) with df degrees of freedom. This value needs to be looked up and can be evaluate in R using the qchisq() function. See the help file here for more details. 8.7 Resampling methods for frequentist estimation The methods for estimating confidence intervals in this section rely on assumptions that the statistic’s sampling distribution follows a normal or t-distribution. We may be not be able to justify this assumption in some cases, or it might be difficult to derive an unbiased sample estimator. Without any other information, our best guess as to the distribution of the population is the observations in our sample. 8.7.1 Bootstrap A bootstrap estimator is determined by randomly by resampling the data with replacement to create many new hypothetical data sets each with the same sample size. We calculate our statistic of interest for each of the many resampled (with replacement) hypothetical data sets. The bootstrap estimate of the parameter is the mean of these statistics. The SE of the bootstrap estimate is their SD. Confidence intervals for bootstrap methods are: percentile method, the bias corrected method, and the accelerated bootstrap (see Efron and Hastie 2016). Efron and Hastie recommended at least 2,000 samples for confidence interval estimation using bootstrap methods. The percentile method involves ranking the estimated statistic values for each sample. If there are 1000 samples, the 95\(\%\) confidence interval is estimated as [25th ranked estimate, 975th estimate]. Example of resampled (with replacement) data sets for the pea length data: pea.length = t(pea.length) # sample() function only works when pea.length is a row vector. pea.length # print original pea length data for reference ## length1 length2 length3 length4 length5 length6 length7 length8 length9 ## [1,] 65 67 68 70 71 75 76 74 72 ## length10 length11 ## [1,] 68 66 # Make samples sample1 <- sample(pea.length, replace = TRUE) sample2 <- sample(pea.length, replace = TRUE) sample3 <- sample(pea.length, replace = TRUE) sample4 <- sample(pea.length, replace = TRUE) sample5 <- sample(pea.length, replace = TRUE) resampled.data = data.frame(sample1, sample2, sample3, sample4, sample5) resampled.data ## sample1 sample2 sample3 sample4 sample5 ## 1 65 68 72 68 75 ## 2 67 68 75 71 68 ## 3 65 67 68 66 66 ## 4 74 68 67 75 66 ## 5 72 74 76 72 75 ## 6 65 74 74 68 75 ## 7 66 68 67 65 67 ## 8 76 68 76 75 70 ## 9 71 72 72 68 65 ## 10 65 74 66 65 72 ## 11 70 70 71 68 76 8.7.2 Jackknife The jackknife is an earlier alternative to bootstrapping that is less computer intensive. 9 Fri Sept 25 (A2 due) - Hypothesis testing (frequentist) and Bayesian statistics 9.1 Hypothesis testing (frequentist) Mayo (2018) summarizes the hypothesis testing process as: A hypothesis, typically about the value of a parameter, \(\theta\), that reflects some biological process affecting the data. We make assumptions, via models, when we express our hypotheses in terms of parameter values. A “distance function”, calculated from the data that will allow to assess how well the data fits the model (or mathematical representation of your hypothesis). We we calculate the expected distribution of the “distance function” under the hypothesis we call this a test statistic. A decision rule, to determine if the test statistic value calculated for our data and model, is consistent with the hypothesis. Biological versus statistical significance. If we find the differences between mean snail weights between two populations is 1\(\%\), this result might be statistically significant (particularly if the sample size is large), but the result might not be biologically meaningful. We need to considered the specific biology to know if an effect is biologically significant. For example, for toxins, a small difference could be biologically meaningful, but for other biological question, i.e. snail weights, a small difference, even when statistically significant, might not be biologically meaningful. 9.1.1 Frequentist statistical hypothesis testing The frequentist approach, developed by RA Fisher, involves the following steps: Construct a null hypothesis, \(H_0\), i.e., there amount of phosphorous in corn does not depending of soil phosphorous, i.e., \(\beta_1 = 0\), where \(\beta_1\) is the slope of a hypothesiszed linear relationship. Choose a test statistic that will compare our sample slope value (\(b_1\)) to that predicted (\(\beta_1 = 0\)) and generate a standard error from our data. This case, given our null hypothesis, the test statistic \((b_1 - 0)/s_b\) will follow a t-distribution with \(n-2\) df. Fishers’ test rule compares the test statistic from the data to values expected from such samples when \(H_0\) is correct. A test statistic beyond a threshold is evidence for rejecting the null hypothesis. A key component of the framework is the p-value. A p-value of \(0.01\) means only a 1\(\%\) chance of obtaining these data if the null hypothesis were correct. The p-value is \(P(\mbox{data}|H_0)\), i.e. the probability of observing these data given the null hypothesis. Fisher’s approach was extended by Neyman-Pearson to consider an alternative hypothesis, \(H_1\) (referred to as the N-P framework). Fisher’s approach notes that we might falsely reject the null hypothesis when it is actually correct (termed type I (or alpha) error). In the N-P framework, another possibility is that the alternative hypothesis is falsely rejected (termed type II (or beta) error) due to random chance for these particular data there were collected. 9.1.2 Decision errors See Type I and Type II errors here. Traditionally, biologists have been concerned about Type I errors, i.e., not claiming an effect when none exists. The idea was that the discipline is protected by ensuring that we do not accept falsely correct hypotheses. Historically, \(\alpha = 0.05\%\) was considered an acceptable type I error and an effect could only be claimed as statistically significant if the p-value for our analysis was less than \(0.05\). A smaller value of \(\alpha\) might protect against claiming false effects even more, but a problem with protecting against type I errors is that doing so increases the chance of Type II errors. In environmental assessment or experimetns involving human health, controlling type II errors may be more important than controlling type I errors. A type II error is failure to detect an effect that has occurred. Good sampling design should protect against both errors, primarily by taking large enough samples to be confident in our estimates and conclusions. Statistical power, \(1-\beta\), is the probability of \(H_1\) generating a test-statistic above the critical value, leading to \(H_0\) being correctly rejected. 9.1.3 Parameteric tests and their assumptions Tests, i.e. t-tests and ANOVA, that specify a probability distribution for the variable from which our samples came and the test statistic are referred to as ‘parametric tests’. If the assumptions of any statistical test are not met, the parameter estimates and confidence intervals may be unreliable and the statistical decisions that are reached may be incorrect. When assumptions, such as that data arise from normally-distributed populations, observations are independent and sampled randomly form the same populations, and/or that group comparisons have equal variance are not met, we can consider robust tests, randomization procedures, and rank-based methods. 9.1.4 Comments on frequentist inference Frequentist inference has long been the dominant approach in biology, health, environmental sciences, and other disciplines. More recently aspects of the frequentist approach, particularly null hypothesis statistical testing, have been intensely debated and criticized. This prompted the American Statistical Association to release a state on P-values’, context, process and purpose (Wasserstein and Lazar, 2016). See Ellison et al. 2014 for an ecologically oriented discussion. Some of the criticisms are warranted, but all statistical approaches have limitations when scrutinized. It has been pointed out that researchers would prefer an interval that covers 95\(\%\) of possible parameter values rather than a confidence interval. This can be achieved with Bayesian credible intervals. Similarly, we might prefer a probability that a hypothesis is true such as \(H_0\) is true, but rather than that p-values quantify the probability of getting our sample data, or data more extreme from repeated sampling from our populations is the \(H_0\) is true. A conclusion from the discussions in the literature has been that p-values, if interpreted correctly and in combination with effect sizes (interpretted in terms of biological significance), can be appropriate. A threshold value, such as \(\alpha = 0.05\) has been criticized. The frequentist approach is not well-suited to incorporating prior knowledge. 9.2 Bayesian statistical inference Unlike frequentist statistics, Bayesian inference makes a philosophical shift in how we understand parameters and probabilities. In Bayesian statistics we understand the parameters of interest to be random variables that can take a range of values, each with different probabilities representing our degrees of belief. This contrast with the frequentist view that population parameters are fixed, but unknown. For Bayesian inference, we also understand probabilities as degrees of belief, rather than the long range frequency of events (which is the frequentist interpretation). In Bayesian statistics, \[ P(\theta|\mbox{data}) = \dfrac{P(\mbox{data}|theta)P(\theta)}{P(\mbox{data})}, \] where \(\theta\) is our parameter to be estimated to assess the hypothesis, \(P(\theta)\) is our prior probability distribution of the parameter value (not considering our data), and \(P(\theta|\mbox{data})\) is the posterior probability, which the probability the \(\theta\) is equal to a particular value given our data and our prior beliefs. \(P(\mbox{data}|theta)\) is the probability of observing the data for a given value of \(\theta\) and \(P(\mbox{data})\) is the probability of observing the data and is normalization (so that the area under the probability distriubtion is 1). 9.2.1 Prior knowledge and probability Priors can be strongly or weakly informative of the parameter of interest. A weakly informative prior has a large variance, and can be an overly conservative interpretation of prior knowledge. A non-informative prior, i.e. a uniform distribution across a large range, implies that there is no prior knowledge of the parameter value and a frequentist approach is equivalent and appropriate. A strongly informative prior will have substantial impact on the estimated posterior distribution of the parameter of interest. It is very important that biologists explain their derivation of their prior when using Bayesian inference. Conclusions in Bayesian statistics are based on the posterior probability. It is necessary to use computationally intensive interative methoes (i.e., Markov chain Monte Carlo, MCMC) to estimate the posterior probability given data and a prior distribution. The most common MCMC method used to obtain the posterior probability is the Gibbs sampler. The mean of the posterior distribution is our parameter estimate when using Bayesian inference. Bayesian credible intervals are the analog of frequentist confidence intervals, but the credible intervals are interpretted differently. The 95\(\%\) credible intervals are two values of the parameter between which 95\(\%\) of the posterior probability lies. The credible intervals are interpretted as a 95\(\%\) probability that the parameter falls within this range. The credible intervals are a statement about the parameter, while frequentist confidence intervals are a statement about the parameter. Credible intervals can be assymetric. 9.2.2 Example For an example that uses some Bayesian methods, see Anokye et al. 2026. Quantifying SARS-CoV-2 Omicron variant spread and the impact of non-pharmaceutical interventions in Newfoundland and Labrador, Canada. PLOS Computational Biology and particularly Table 1 in the main text (which reports credible intervals) and Section S1.6 in the Supplementary Information which explains the Bayesian parameter estimation and visualizes the prior and posterior distributions. 9.2.3 Final comments In the course, as in the Quinn and Keough textbook we describe the frequentist approach to statistics. This is because without strongly informative priors, the Bayesian point estimates and credible intervals will be close to their frequentist analogs. We recognize the limitation of frequentist statistics in not being able to incorporate prior knowledge. Quinn and Keough view prior information as most valuable when used to frame, rather than answer, research questions. 9.3 Reading Ch 2.5 - 2.7 in Quinn and Keough.

10 Mon Sept 28 - Sampling and experimental design and power analysis 10.1 Sampling design 10.2 Sample size for random sampling 10.3 Non-probability sampling 10.4 Experimential design 10.5 Sample size for detecting differences: power analysis 10.6 Readings

10 Mon Sept 28 - Sampling and experimental design and power analysis 10.1 Sampling design 10.1.1 Probability sampling Statistical population: Populations are all possible units and their associated observations of interest. Samples are a collection of observations from a population. The number of units in the sample is the sample size. Distinct from biological population (same species). Sampling error arise because any observation will be an imperfect representation of the population and is measured by the standard error: the standard deviation of a sample statistic based on repeated sampling. For probability sampling, the probabilities of selecting individual sampling units are known. Simple random sampling For a given sample size, \(n\), all possible sampling units in the population have an equal chance of being selected. Can be achieved by giving all sampling units an identifier and using a random number generator. Examples: randomly select animals in a population, or overlay a spatial grid. Simple random sampling is always the goal, but it may be more expensive. Formula for means, variances, SE, and CIs assume simple random sampling. Stratified sampling The population is partitioned into levels that represent clearly defined groups (or strata) of units. Under stratified sampling we sample independently and randomly from each group. There are different formulas for calculative the population mean and the standard error of the population mean when stratified sampling is used. The group/strata should be included in statistical models as a predictor variable. Examples of groups/strata: pool vs. riffle in a stream; or grassland, woodlood, wetland etc. We might want to sample equally, or in proportion to the area, of these habitats. Cluster sampling Modifies simple random sampling to account for heterogeneity. Simple cluster sampling involves sampling all secondary units (i.e., branches) from within the randomly selected primary unit (i.e., tree). Sytematic sampling involves choosing sampling units that are equally spaced in time or in space. A limitation is that is is not possible to calculate an unbiased estimate of sampling variance and standard error. Another limitation is that unknown regularity may coincide with sampling. Unequal probability sampling may be useful to select units based on their size. Adaptive sampling sampling design is based on initial observations. 10.2 Sample size for random sampling If we have some estimate of the variability between the sampling units in our population, we can estimate the sample size required to for any sample mean to be within some bounds around the true mean given repeated sampling. Specifically, \[ n \geq \frac{z^2s^2}{d^2}, \] where \(z\) is the value from a standard normal distribution for a given level of confidence (i.e., \(z=1.96\) for 95\(\%\) confidence interval), \(s^2\) is the estimate of the variance of the population (i.e., from a pilot study), and \(d\) is the maximum allowable absolute difference between the estimated and true population means. This formula is for the mean, but comparable formula are availble for other statistics. These calculations are different/more difficult for other sampling designs (i.e. stratified sampling, systematic sampling). 10.3 Non-probability sampling Convenience sampling i.e., sampling streams near bridges, or forests near campus. Haphazard sampling Mimics random sampling trying to avoid bias, however, our biases usually affect the choices (i.e., not getting feet wet, or walking all the way up a hill). Purposive sampling i.e., people are selected because researchers judge them to be representative of the population. 10.4 Experimential design Manipulative experiments have a treatment structure (i.e., treatment and control). The sets of related treatments are termed factors. The smallest unit to which an experimental treatment can be applied are experimental units. The design structure determines how the factor groups (i.e., different treatments) are applied to the experimental units. Confounding is differences in the treatment effects cannot be separated from extraneous factors, i.e., a hormone treatment is applied only to female crayfish. Note that confounding is generally not this easy to identify. Replication of experimental units Replication is having multiple experimental/sampling units for each experimental treatment. Replication is necessary because biological systems are noisy. Without replication, confounding is very likely. Increasing replication by increasing observational, rather than experimental (treatment level) units, could result in pseudo-replication. For example, increasing the number of fish in a tank, rather than the number of tanks to which the treatment is applied, or increasing the number of tree samples taken within a burned area, instead of adding a new burn area to measure in. To avoid confounding, think about the unit to which the treatment is applied. This is the experimental unit. If we take multiple measurements within an experimental unit, it is recommended to take the mean of these measurements before doing the statistics to avoid confounding. Controls allow us to measure that a change would not have occurred without the treatment. This is stronger evidence of a treatment effect as it reduces the chance of confounding. Randomization random treatments should be sufficiently interspersed, for example, all treatment one (carbon subsidy) replicates occurs first along a gradient (i.e., upstream), and all treatment two (i.e., nitrogen subsidy) occur second along the gradient (see Figure 3.3 on p37 of Quinn and Keough). If this occurs, you should re-randomize, but in doing so it is necessary to decide on an acceptible level of interspersion a priori (i.e., before). Independence lack of independence between experimental units can bias conclusions or complicate analysis. For example, treatment spreads downstream. Reducing unexplained variance. Good experimental design aims to detect a signal and minimize unexplained variance. This could occur by including additional predictor variables, or narrowing the scope of the population form which the samples are drawn. Limitations of manipulative experiments Manipulative experiments can introduce artifacts themselves. Extending inference beyond the experiment requires caution. Before-After-Control-Impact is a common approach used in environmental impact assessment. 10.5 Sample size for detecting differences: power analysis Power is the probability of detecting an effect with our sample(s), if it occurs in the population(s). Power, \(1-\beta\), is the complement of type II error, \(\beta\), and \[ \mbox{Power} \propto \dfrac{\mbox{ES}\alpha\sqrt{n}}{\sigma}, \] where \(\mbox{ES}\) is the effect size (the size of the effect we want to be able to detect - units are the same as the quantity we are measuring), \(n\) is the sample size, \(\sigma^2\) is the variation between experimental or sampling units, and \(\alpha\) is a desired significance level (often choose as 0.05). Also, the acceptable level of Type I error. Using power analysis to plan experiments (a prior power analysis) Most commonly used to estimate how many samples are needed, given a desired level of power, for specified values of \(\alpha\) and effect size and an estimate of variance. If the number of samples is fixed, we could calculate the magnitude of the ES we can detected with a given power, i.e., minimum detectable effect size (MDES). This might be an option if you cannot specify an effect size a priori. See Box 3.1 and Figure 3.4 in Quinn and Keough. Sequence of steps: 1. State clearly the effects to be observed if little or no effect occurs, and if a biologically meaningful effect is observed. Identify the statistical model to be applied to the data and sate the desired power and decision criteria. Identify the assumptions of the statistical model. Use a comparable data analysis as a guide. If you expect to transform data, express the ES on the transformed scale. Estimate the variance in the variable to be analyzed (the variation between replicates). Consider published studies and/or a pilot study. The variability estimate should be on spatial and temporal scales similar to your planned data collection. There is no reason to think that variability estimates will translate between scales. If there is a constraint on sample size, we can calculate MDES. Post hoc power calculation Calculating observed power tells us nothing new. We could make recommendations for future experiments and this requires defining the ES we wished to detect. Effect size is a critical step in power analysis. This is a biological judgement. The more complex the statistical design the more difficult it is to calculate the effect size. See Nakagawa and Cuthill (2007) and Ialongo (2016) for some common effect sizes. Using power analysis A priori power analysis should be a routine part of data analysis, even if researchers do not plan to make inferences based on “statistical significance”. If you cannot take the number of samples needed, you might still proceed with your data collection, but it is a gamble. You might consider a lower value of acceptable type I error (\(\alpha\)). Key points Getting answers to biological questions invovles: designing data collection to separate competing explanations, collecting data that are representative of statistical populations, collecting enough data to be confident in conclusions. Random sampling should be the default approach. Confounding can occur when appropriate controls are missing. Confounding also occurs with inappropriate replication at the level of the experiment treatment, i.e., pseuo-replication (Hurlbert 2009). Quinn and Keough recommend summarizing multiple observational units within the same replicate or sampling unit (i.e., by calculating the mean). Quinn and Keough also strongly recommend calcuating the appropriate number of samples before collecting data. This is the number necessary to estimate a parameter with a target confidence or an effect of a particular size (which is achieve with a power analysis). 10.6 Readings Ch 3 Quinn and Keough.

11 Fri Oct 2 (Quiz 2) - What is a linear model and how to assess model fit 11.1 Last 20 minutes: Quiz 2 11.2 What is a linear model? \[\begin{eqnarray} (\mbox{response variable})_i & =& \qquad (\mbox{linear predictors})_i \qquad \qquad \qquad \ + (\mbox{random error})_i, \\ y_i \qquad &=& \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{1,i} + \beta_2 x_{2,i} + \dots + \beta_n x_{n,i} \qquad + \epsilon_i. \end{eqnarray}\] For linear models, predictor variables and their parameters are combined as a linear combination. The predictor variables maybe continuous (i.e., classical regression models) or categorial (i.e., classical regression model). Predictor variables may also be fixed (infererence restricted to the values used) or random (inference generalized to a broader population, i.e., where the variable corresponds to individuals or sites). For linear models: - the response variable should reflect the biological question and be measurable; - all predictor variables that are biological relevant should be measureed and included in the model; - the model should generalize to the population from which the observations came. These can be achieved by applying our biological knowledge and using an appropriate sampling strategy. 11.2.1 Response variables For continuous response variables, a normal distribution underlies OLS estimation for these types of variables. Biological data can often be right-skewed such that log-normal transformation might be considered. Discrete response variables might be binary (i.e., nominal) for example presence/absence or dead/alive. Binary response variables are usually modelled with a binomial distribution. Discrete response variables might be counts and modelled with a Poisson distribution. If data is over-dispersed (mean not equal to the variance) then a negative binomial can be used (see 13.6.2 in Quinn and Keough). 11.3 Readings Ch 4.1-4.2 Quinn and Keough.

12 Mon Oct 05 - Linear model fitting and how well does a linear model fit? 12.1 Assembing our linear model 12.2 Estimation and fit for linear models 12.3 Readings

12 Mon Oct 05 - Linear model fitting and how well does a linear model fit? 12.1 Assembing our linear model \[\begin{eqnarray} (\mbox{response variable}) & =& \qquad (\mbox{linear predictors}) \qquad \qquad \qquad \ + (\mbox{random error}), \\ y \qquad &=& \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{1} + \beta_2 x_{2} + \dots + \beta_n x_{n} \qquad + \epsilon. \end{eqnarray}\] The linear model has a: Random component, \(\epsilon\). For the general linear model this is the normal distribution; Systematic component. For the linear model this the sum of the predictor variables, and their associated parameters (including the intercept \(\beta_0\)); Link function, which links the random and the systematic components. The link function essentially transforms the response variable so the transformed response variable has a linear relationship with the predictors. For general linear models the link function is the identity function (\(\mu = f(\mu)\), i.e., no link function is needed). Other link functions are log (\(\log(\mu_i)\)) and logit (\(\log(\mu_i/(1-\mu_i))\)) which are used for Poisson regression, loglinear models, and binary and proportion responses in logistic regression. 12.2 Estimation and fit for linear models Our estimators should be BLUE: best linear unbiased estimators. Two estimation methods are ordinary least squares (OLS) and maximum likelihood (ML) estimation. 12.2.1 Ordinary least squares Minimize the sum of the squared deviations. Also called residual or error sums-of-squares (\(\mbox{SS}_{\mbox{Residual}}\)) where, \[ \mbox{SS}_{\mbox{Residual}} = \sum_{i=1}^n(y_i - \hat{y})^2\]. Here, \(\hat{y}\) are the fitted values of \(y\), the response variable (or the values of \(y\) predicted by the fitted model). The fitted model is the one that minimizes the residual, and has fitted values of the intercept \(\hat{\beta}_0\) and the slopes, \(\hat{\beta}_1\), \(\hat{\beta}_2\), etc. Additionally, we also wish to estimate \(\sigma^2_{\epsilon}\), the variance of the error terms. The error variance is often abbreviated to \(\sigma^2\), and is the unexplained variance for the model. The unexplained variance measures how well our model fits the data and is used to estimate confidence intervals for parameters. OLS is usually more straightforward that ML estimation. The R function lm() is an implementation of OLS to estimate the BLUE parameters for general linear models. OLS measures of fit: ANOVA To test hypothesis that parameters are equal to zero, we can use a t-test. We can also compare the fit of the model with the parameter fitted (termed the full model) to the fit of the model with the parameter set equal to zero (termed the reduced model). When there is a single response variable we partition the total variation in the response variable into that explained by the model (i.e., the one predictor variable) and the unexplained variance (residual or error variance) using an ANOVA. The ratio of the two variances is an F-statistic. The term ANOVA is commonly used by biologists (and some statistical textbooks) to refer to a specific class of linear models with categorical predictors and a normally-distributed response variable. This can be misleading - while ANOVA is used to analyzie such models, it broadly applies to all linear models based on OLS regression (including classical regression models with continuous predictor variables. For example, x <- seq(0,4) data = data.frame(x = x, y=x+rnorm(5,0,1)) data ## x y ## 1 0 0.680258 ## 2 1 1.069339 ## 3 2 3.209522 ## 4 3 2.878359 ## 5 4 4.244875 mod = lm(y~x, data=data) mod ## ## Call: ## lm(formula = y ~ x, data = data) ## ## Coefficients: ## (Intercept) x ## 0.6288 0.8938 anova_table<-anova(mod) anova_table ## Analysis of Variance Table ## ## Response: y ## Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr(>F) ## x 1 7.9892 7.9892 23.377 0.01687 * ## Residuals 3 1.0253 0.3418 ## --- ## Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 We apply the anova() function to the fitted linear regression mod to test the null hypothesis that the population variances estimated by the two mean squares (\(\mbox{MS}_{\mbox{Explained}}\) and \(\mbox{MS}_{\mbox{Residual}}\)) are the same. The result is the ANOVA table for our linear regression. The ANOVA table has the following characteristics: \(\mbox{df}_{\mbox{Explained}} +\mbox{df}_{\mbox{Residual}} = \mbox{df}_{\mbox{Total}} = n-1\) (where \(n\) is the sample size); \(\mbox{SS}_{\mbox{Explained}} +\mbox{SS}_{\mbox{Residual}} = \mbox{SS}_{\mbox{Total}}\); \(\mbox{MS}_{\mbox{Explained}} = \mbox{SS}_{\mbox{Explained}}/\mbox{df}_{\mbox{Explained}}\) and \(\mbox{MS}_{\mbox{Residual}} = \mbox{SS}_{\mbox{Residual}}/\mbox{df}_{\mbox{Residual}}\) (where MS is the mean square); and The F-statistic is calculated as \(F = \mbox{MS}_{\mbox{Explained}} / \mbox{MS}_{\mbox{Residual}}\). The \(\mbox{SS}_{\mbox{Total}}\) for the data and model above is: # Sum the 'Sum Sq' column to get SST SSTotal <- sum(anova_table$"Sum Sq") SSTotal ## [1] 9.014528 For each of the bullet points, check that the ANOVA table satifies the formula that are given. 12.2.2 Maximum likelihood The maximum likelihood parameter estimates maximize the likelihood of observing our data. Maximum likelihood methods do not need to use normally distributed errors. ML measures of fit: log-likelihood and deviance Evaluating hypothesis (i.e., that parameter values are equal to 0) can be done done using the likelihood-ratio test. The likelihood ratio test statistic, \(\lambda\), is, \[ \lambda = -2(LL_0 - LL_1), \] where \(LL_0\) is the log-likelihood of the reduced model and \(LL_1\) is the log-likelihood of the full model. The log-likelhood is the calculated by taking the natural logarithm of likelihood. The likelihoods are often numbers less than 1, and so the log-likelihoods are often negative numbers. A large likelihood corresponds to a good fit, and so does a large log-likelihood. When the full model is much more likely than the reduced model then \(LL_0 - LL_1\) is large and negative, which corresponds to a large positive value of \(\lambda\). The likelihood ratio test statistic, \(\lambda\), follows a \(\chi^2\) distribution if the sample sizes are not too small and this can be used to test hypotheses. The fit of ML measures is usually assessed by calculating the deviance. A saturated model is a model that has the same number of parameters as data points and explains all the variation in the response variable. The deviance is calculated as, \[ D = 2(LL_S - LL_1) \] where \(LL_S\) is the log-likelihood of the saturated model and \(LL_1\) is the log-likelihood of our model. A large deviance means the fit of our model is poor. 12.2.3 Information criterion The term “ordinary” least squares is because there are other types of least squares. Information criteria such as Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) and Bayesian information criteria (BIC) are types of penalized least squares that can involve minimizing the least squares and also including a term that penalizes unncessary model complexity. The AIC value for a model is calculated as, \[ -2(\mbox{LL}_i - p_i) \] where \(\mbox{LL}_i\) is the log-likelihood of the model \(i\) and \(p_i\) is the number of parameters in model \(i\). AIC is used for non-nested models, when the likelihood ratio test cannot be used. If a model is nested it means that it can be obtained by setting a parameter in another model to 0. 12.3 Readings Ch4.3-4.5 Quinn and Keough

13 Wed Oct 07 - Exploratory data analysis Today’s lecture material will not be on Exam I. 13.1 Introduction to linear models (continued) Errors and residuals: Errors are the difference between the observation and the population value. Residuals are the difference between the observation and the estimated value. 13.1.1 Assumptions for linear model inference OLS assumes independent identically distributed errors, and specifically, that the identical distributions are normal distributions with a mean of 0 and constant variance, \(\sigma^2\). Violations can result in inaccurate confidence intervals and p-values, although OLS is reasonably robust, at lest to non-normality and unequal variance. Assumptions of: Zero conditional means of errors. Check by plotting the residuals against the predictors. Independence of errors. The assumption strictly refers to independence of the model error terms, but it is often described as the independence of the observations, because correlated/non-independent observations usually result in non-independent errors. Test with a plot of the residuals against the predictors and look for obvious positive, negative, or cyclical trends. If spatial autocorrelation is the concern, make a variogram (Dale and Fortin 2009). Homogeneity of error variances (homoskedasticity). Heteroskedasticity (non-equal variances) often results when the underlying model error distribution is non-normal. Can also be due to outliers. Plot residuals against the predictor values, and look for unequal spread of the residuals. For categorical variables plot the residuals against the group means. Normality of errors. Assumption is that errors are normally distributed, but usually this means that response variables are normally distributed. Normality assumptions can be assessed with Q-Q plot (compares the quantiles of the data to the quantiles of a normal distribution), but statistical inference is generally robust to violations of the assumption of normally distributed errors and many statisticians do not view this assumption as a critical issue (Gelman and Hill 2006, cited on p57 of Quinn and Keough). 13.1.2 Types of linear model (General and generalized) These are the most common types of linear models used by biologists.l General linear models are also commonly just called linear models. The response variable is continuous and has an underlying normal distribution. Use the identity link function. Continuous predictor variables: Regression. This analysis is known as a regression, and the equation for the fitted regression is: \[ \hat{y}_i = b_0 + b_1x_i \] where \(\hat{y}_i\) are the fitted (or model-predicted) response variable values (i.e., as you did in assignment 2) and \(b_0\) and \(b_1\) are the fitted (or estimated) intercept and slope. If \(b_1\) is not different from 0 then this predictor variable, \(x_i\) explains very little of the variation that was measured in the response variable. Categorical predictor variables: ANOVA. This analysis is known as ANOVA. As the preditor variables are discrete we might plot our data as boxplots (or violin plots etc). The equation for an ANOVA is: \[ y_{ij} = \mu + \alpha_i + \epsilon_{ij} \] where \(i\) is category \(i\) and \(j\) is a particular observation. The effect of category \(i\) is measured as \(\alpha_i\), which is written as being additive with respect to the mean \(\mu\), which is calculated by taking the mean by considering the observations across all the categories (i.e. ignoring the categories). The term \(\epsilon_{ij}\) represents error for the observation \(i\) in category \(j\). The group (or category mean) is \(\mu_i = \mu + \alpha_i\). Software packages often implement and report ANOVA as: \[ \hat{y}_{i} = b_0 + b_1 \mathbb{1}_{i=1} + \dots + b_{m-1} \mathbb{1}_{i=m-1} \] which says that the estimated mean of category \(i\) (the fitted parameter estimate) is \(\hat{y}_i\) where \(b_0\) is the estimated mean of the reference category (arbitrarily choosen and labelled \(i=0\)) and \(i \in {0, 1, \dots, m-1}\) are estimates for the other \(m-1\) categorical variable means (relative to the mean of the reference category). \(\mathbb{1}_{i=j}\) is an indicator variable that is 1 when we are considering catergory \(i = j\) and 0 otherwise. This means that the formula to calculate the fitted value of \(\hat{y}_i\) for a particular category is \(b_0\) for the reference category or \(\hat{y}_i=b_0 + b_j\) for any of the other categories. It does not matter which of the \(m\) categorical variables are indexed by \(0, 1\) or any of the other numbers up to \(m-1\). Generalized linear models include: Logistic regression: binary response; continuous predictor variables Possion regression: Poisson response; continuous predictor variables Contingency tables: Response is classified by two or more categorical variables. Question is about correlation or independence, i.e., 2 x 2 \(\chi^2\) test for independence or deviation from an expected pattern. Linear mixed models. Predictor variables are modelled as fixed and random effects. 13.2 Exploratory analysis 13.2.1 Basic graphical tools We wish to understand the shape of the distribution of our sample data, particularly model residuals, which we can explore by graphing the shape of the distribution of our response variable. Basic common graphs: histogram, dotplot, boxplot (and violin plot), probability plot (p-p and q-q), scatterplot, and scatterplot matrix. Smoothing (i.e., LOESS or LOWESS) Residual plots 13.2.2 Outliers Quinn and Keough argue that outliers are best identified by exploratory analysis (i.e. box plots) rather than statistical tests. After identifying the outliers, first check it is not a mistake, i.e., an equipment malfunction or data entry error. If you have an outlier, that does not have an explanation (in terms of being anomalous or a mistake), re-run the analysis without the outlier to determine if the outlier impacts the results. Cook’s D-statistic measures how much an observation affects parameter estimation for linear models. You may need to use a statistic test developed for outliers. You should only remove outliers from your data if you have an a priori reason to expect the outlire is an anomaly or a mistake. 13.2.3 Am I fitting the right model? The underlying probability distribution. Inference is often robust to violations of normality assumptions, but we should check for symmetry in response variables and residuals using boxplots and p-p plots. If data is right-skewed, a log-trasformation could be considered, although inference is probably more robust if you instead consider errors following a Poisson distribution (i.e., a Poisson regression) or another distribution using ML estimation. The common probability distributions have one peak. If your response variable is multi-peaked the best approach might be to split your analysis into multiple populations, with separate analysis for each population. Data with many zeros is best split into two processes: no response; and given a response what is it’s value. These statistical methods are called zero-inflated. Homogeneity of variances. Often more important than the assumption of normal errors (or response variables) is the assumption that the normal distribution has constant variance. For the normal distribution, \(\sigma^2\) is an estimated parameter for both OLS and ML. The Poisson distribution has the mean equal to the variance (such that the variance may not be constant), a reason for heteroskedasticity could be that a Poisson error distribution is more consistent with these data. Quinn and Keough recommend graphical approaches to inspect for hetroskedasticity (non-homogeneity of variance), for example box plots. These are preferred to formal tests (although Levene’s test is an option) unless testing for unequal variance is the focal research question. Is a linear model appropriate? Examine this question by making a scatter plot. See also Anscombe (1973). 13.2.4 Is it Normal to transform data? Transforming cm to m illustrates the arbitrary choices that we might make regarding transformations. The conclusions of linear transformations (i.e., cm to m) will be identical. Nonlinear transformations (i.e., taking the logarithm of the response variable) change the research question being addressed by the analysis. Such transformations might be made to meet distributional assumptions of linear model analysis. If you transform your response variable, it has been argued that you should present your results on the transformed scale (i.e., log-growth rather than growth). Another common transformation is to take the squareroot of the response variable. Transformations can also help satisfy linearity assumptions. Nowdays, it is not Normal to transform data. It is generally awkward to frame research questions in terms of “log-growth” or the “square root of growth”. Historically, transformations were needed because estimation with ML was computationally inaccessible. To meet distributional assumptions, it is better to use ML methods which have the flexibility to be formulated for a range of distributions. 13.2.5 Standardizations Standardizations can facilitate comparisons. Changing a variable to have a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1 is a common standardization. 13.2.6 Missing data There are different mechanisms for missingness. One approach to addressing missingness is imputation. 13.3 Readings Ch 4.6-4.7 and Ch 5 Quinn and Keough
