Specifically: Example 9.3.1 from Snedecor and Cochran (1989). The quantity of interest is the phosphorus content of corn (Pcorn in ppm), in relation to the phosphorus levels in samples of soils with experimentally fixed levels of phosphorus (Psoil in ppm) data = read.csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ahurford/biol-4605-data/refs/heads/main/data/corn.csv") data ## Psoil Pcorn ## 1 1 64 ## 2 4 71 ## 3 5 54 ## 4 9 81 ## 5 13 93 ## 6 11 76 ## 7 23 77 ## 8 23 95 ## 9 28 109 There are \(n=9\) observations. Dr. Schneider’s notes initially report only 8 data points in the data table. In some subsequent calculations in Dr. Schneider’s notes sometimes 8 observations are considered and sometimes 9. We will use these 9 data points for all the calculations. Rather than following the analysis from Dr. Schneider’s notes, we apply the analyses from Quinn and Keough. 15.3.1 Exploratory analysis Quinn and Keough recommends fitting a LOESS smoother as an exploratory test to evaluate for a linear relationship. We consider boxplots of the explanatory (predictor) and response variables to look for symmetry, which suggests the residuals likely statisfy the normality assumption. I load ggplot2 and ggExtra to complete this plot of the data. library(ggplot2) library(ggExtra) # 2. Save the base ggplot with the LOESS line main_plot <- ggplot(data, aes(x = Psoil, y = Pcorn)) + geom_point(color = "black") + geom_smooth(method = "loess", span = 0.75, color = "blue", se = FALSE) + theme_minimal() # 3. Add marginal boxplots to the top and right sides final_plot <- ggMarginal( main_plot, type = "boxplot", margins = "both", # Adds to both top and right fill = "lightblue", # Color of the boxplots size = 10 # Relative ratio of main plot size to marginal plot size ) # 4. Display the plot print(final_plot) The LOESS plot can be compared to the analogous plots in Quinn and Keough (Figures 6.1 and 6.2 on p78 and 79). Our smoothed data seems to meet the assumption of linearity. The boxplots indicate no outliers. We can only assess assumptions concerning residuals after fitting a model. # 1. Fit the linear regression model <- lm(Psoil ~ Pcorn, data = data) # 2. Create data frame holding just the predicted and residual values plot_data <- data.frame( predicted = fitted(model), residuals = residuals(model) ) # 3. Build the ggplot ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = predicted, y = residuals)) + geom_point(color = "black") + labs( title = "Residuals vs. Predicted Plot", x = "Predicted Values (Fitted)", y = "Residuals" ) + theme_minimal() We are hoping not to see bowls, arches or cones (see Dr. Schneider’s notes). Bowls and arches might arise from non-linear relationships between the predictor and the response. Cones would indicate heteroskedasticity. This looks like our assumptions of linearity and homoskedasticity are statisfied. Lastly, we can look for outliers. # 1. Create a data frame with Cook's distance values and row names/indices plot_data <- data.frame( observation = rownames(data), # Or use 1:nrow(mtcars) for indices cooks_d = cooks.distance(model) ) # 2. Define a standard threshold rule-of-thumb: 4 / n threshold <- 4 / nrow(data) # 3. Create the ggplot ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = reorder(observation, cooks_d), y = cooks_d)) + geom_segment(aes(xend = observation, yend = 0), color = "gray") + # The sticks geom_point(size = 3) + # The candy dots geom_hline(yintercept = threshold, linetype = "dashed", color = "red", linewidth = 0.8) + coord_flip() + # Flips to horizontal for much easier reading of row names labs( title = "Cook's Distance Plot", subtitle = paste("Red dashed line indicates threshold (4/n) =", round(threshold, 3)), x = "Observation", y = "Cook's Distance", ) + theme_minimal() The Cook’s D test suggests no outliers for the linear model fitted to the data. The conclusion of our exploratory analysis is that it is reasonable to fit a linear model. 15.3.2 Write the model and state the hypothesis Our exploratory analyses suggests that a linear regression is reasonable. Next, we will write our model and our hypothesis by following the steps in Dr. Schneider’s notes. Our model is therefore, \[ P_{corn} = \alpha + \beta_{Psoil} P_{soil} + \epsilon, \] where \(P_{corn}\) is phosphorous in the corn (ppm), \(P_{soil}\) is phosphorous in corn (ppm) and \(\alpha\) (ppm) and \(\beta_{Psoil}\) (unitless) are coefficients in our hypothesized linear relationship that will be estimated during fitting. The term \(\epsilon\) is the residual and we assume these residuals are independent and normally distributed, which we can write as \(\epsilon \sim N(0,\sigma^2)\). Our null hypothesis is that \(\beta_{Psoil} = 0\). This means that there is no effect of soil phosphorous on corn phosphorous. At this point, you should decide to test this hypothesis using OLS or ML, but for pedagogical purposes we will illustrate both. The fitted model is, \[ E[P_{corn}] = \hat{\alpha} + \hat{\beta}_{Psoil} P_{soil}, \] where \(\hat{\alpha}\) and \(\hat{\beta}_{Psoil}\) are the fitted coefficients (using either OLS or ML). We can choose different values of \(P_{soil}\) to predict \(E[P_{corn}]\) (the expected value of \(P_{corn}\) without any noise), given our fitted model. 15.3.3 OLS fit of a linear regression of the Phosphourous data To determine the values of \(\hat{\alpha}\) and \(\hat{\beta}_{Psoil}\) we can minimize the \(SS_{res}\), which is the approach of OLS. We have already completed this OLS fit (when completing the exploratory analysis when we executed the lm() command). We named our model, when the fitting was done using OLS model. To replicate the analysis that is reported in Quinn and Keough (Box 6.1, p77-78), we would like a print out of the estimated regression coefficients and their standard error (to estimate confidence intervals), the correlation coefficient (estimates the proportion of the variance that is unexplained by the model), and an ANOVA table to test our null hypothesis that the population variances estimated by the two mean squares for the model and the residual are the same. The commands below will print out these estimates. summary(model) ## ## Call: ## lm(formula = Psoil ~ Pcorn, data = data) ## ## Residuals: ## Min 1Q Median 3Q Max ## -5.9455 -4.6825 -0.1706 3.1398 11.3720 ## ## Coefficients: ## Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) ## (Intercept) -23.5875 10.3913 -2.27 0.05748 . ## Pcorn 0.4573 0.1274 3.59 0.00886 ** ## --- ## Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 ## ## Residual standard error: 6.075 on 7 degrees of freedom ## Multiple R-squared: 0.648, Adjusted R-squared: 0.5977 ## F-statistic: 12.89 on 1 and 7 DF, p-value: 0.008859 This tells us that the fitted value of the intercept is \(\hat{\alpha} = -23.6\) ppm and the standard error for this estimate is 10.4 ppm. The fitted value of the slope of the relationship between \(P_{corn}\) and \(P_{soil}\) is \(\hat{\beta}_{Psoil} = 0.46\) with a standard error of 0.13. The p-value estimates the Type 1 error associated with this estimate: the probability of estimating a \(t-value\) of this magnitude under the null hypothesis that the true population value is \(\beta_{Psoil} = 0\). This probability is just 0.009, so it is very unlikely that the phosphorous in the soil has no effect on the phosphorous in the corn for this experiment. In this print out the Multiple R-squared (\(R^2\)) is the coefficient of determination, and describes the proportion of variance in the response variable that is explained by the model. For our output, the linear model explains about 64.8% of the variance. The correlation coefficient is \(\pm \sqrt{\mbox{Multiple R-squared}}\). The Adjusted R-squared is a modified version of \(R^{2}\) that penalizes the score for every extra predictor variable you add to the model. We would like to better understand the partitioning of the variance in the response variable in terms of the residual or error (unexplained variance) and the variance explained by the model, as well as the degrees of freedom for each. This is the sum squares table: anova(model) ## Analysis of Variance Table ## ## Response: Psoil ## Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr(>F) ## Pcorn 1 475.64 475.64 12.887 0.008859 ** ## Residuals 7 258.36 36.91 ## --- ## Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 We can calculate \(R^2\) as \(SS_{model}\)/\(SS_{Total}\) (from Dr. Schneider’s notes). SSmodel = anova(model)$`Sum Sq`[1] SSTotal = sum(anova(model)$`Sum Sq`) R2 = SSmodel/SSTotal R2 ## [1] 0.6480077 We should also partition our degrees of freedom. This is nicely explained in Dr. Schneider’s notes as: \[ \begin{array}{llll} P_{corn} - \alpha & = & \beta_{Psoil} Psoil & + \ \ \epsilon \\ \mbox{df}_{Total} & = & \mbox{df}_{Model} & + \ \ \mbox{df}_{res} \\ n - 1 & = & 1 & + \ \ \mbox{df}_{res} \\ 8 & = & 1 & + \ \ 7 \\ \end{array} \] Which is how we estimate 7 degrees of freedom for the residual (error) term. Our calculations show that 1 degree of freedom is used to estimate each of the slope and the intercept, and the df associated with the intercept is counted in the total sum of squares (\(SS_{Total}\)). Our analysis suggest the null hypothesis of no effect is unlikely, but we should plot our data and our fitted model: \[ E[P_{corn}] = -23.6 + 0.46 P_{soil} \] as this plot should support and solidify our findings: ggplot(data = data, aes(x = Psoil, y = Pcorn)) + geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, # Fit and overlay a linear model color = "blue", fill = "lightblue", # Customize line and ribbon colors se = TRUE) + # TRUE includes the 95% confidence interval geom_point(color = "black", size = 2) + # Add data points labs( title = "Linear Regression Fit", x = "Soil Phosphorous, Psoil (ppm)", y = "Corn Phosphorous, Pcorn (ppm)" ) + theme_minimal() This plot includes 95\(\%\) CIs for both the slope and the intercept, and so the resulting 95\(\%\) CI for the model has a bow-shape (i.e., fans out at the edges). Recall the interpretation of the CI: this interval has a 95\(\%\) chance of containing the true value of \(P_{corn}\) for any given value of \(P_{soil}\). We can recover the 95\(\%\) CIs for our fitted parameters as: confint(model) ## 2.5 % 97.5 % ## (Intercept) -48.1589386 0.9839166 ## Pcorn 0.1560901 0.7585977 15.3.4 MLE of linear model coefficients and LRT. Maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) is an alternative to OLS and involves defining a likelihood function. If we assume normally distributed errors our fitting is the same as OLS and the lm() function will estimate the log-likelihood for the fitted model. logLik(model) ## 'log Lik.' -27.87757 (df=3) We can compare models by calculating the likelihood ratio. We can fit our null hypothesis as a reduced model: reduced.model = lm(Pcorn ~ 1,data=data) summary(reduced.model) ## ## Call: ## lm(formula = Pcorn ~ 1, data = data) ## ## Residuals: ## Min 1Q Median 3Q Max ## -26 -9 -3 13 29 ## ## Coefficients: ## Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) ## (Intercept) 80.00 5.62 14.23 5.78e-07 *** ## --- ## Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 ## ## Residual standard error: 16.86 on 8 degrees of freedom logLik(reduced.model) ## 'log Lik.' -37.66477 (df=2) The reduced model involves setting \(\beta_{Psoil} = 0\) and only and intercept is estimated. Additionally, likelihood ratio test statistic is calculated form the log-likelihoods as: -2*(logLik(reduced.model) - logLik(model)) ## 'log Lik.' 19.57439 (df=2) The likelihood ratio test statistic follows a Chi-squared distribution. We can use the package lmtest to perform a likelihood ratio test: library(lmtest) # Perform the Likelihood Ratio Test lrtest(reduced.model, model) ## Likelihood ratio test ## ## Model 1: Pcorn ~ 1 ## Model 2: Psoil ~ Pcorn ## #Df LogLik Df Chisq Pr(>Chisq) ## 1 2 -37.665 ## 2 3 -27.878 1 19.574 9.676e-06 *** ## --- ## Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 We find that the full model is more likely than the reduced model given the data. Model fit is usually assessed for ML by calculating the deviance, but this requires fitting a fully saturated model, and we will do this another time. The likelihood ratio for this situation (OLS) in Dr. Schneider’s notes is calculated as: \[ LR = \left(SS_{res}/SS_{total}\right)^{-n/2} \] where the term inside the parenthesis is \(1-R^2\), which is the proportion of the variance which is unexplained (equal to 1 - the proportion of the variance that is explained by the model). n = nobs(model) # Number of observations SSres = SSTotal - SSmodel # Residual sum of squares LR = (SSres/SSTotal)^(-n/2) LR ## [1] 109.7996 Here are some additional notes from Dr. Schneider about interpreting the LR (see p17) that is calculated. Dr. Schneider interprets the likelihood ratio as the strength of evidence to support one model over another. He contrasts evidence with “uncertainty”, which he states is what is measured by the p-value. Dr. Schneider also recommends interpretting the strength of evidence as: LR < 10: inadequate evidence LR > 10: some evidence LR > 20: good evidence LR > 100: strong evidence LR > 1000: very strong evidence 15.3.5 Reporting and interpretting the analysis Dr. Schneider’s notes involve several more steps. This includes making a statement about whether the sample is representative of the population. Reporting the science conclusion is important. All of our analyses, and our graph of the model fit, indicate that the null hypothesis of no effect of soil phosphorous on corn phosphorous can be rejected. Additionally, we should discuss the effect size. Specifically, we estimate that a one unit increase in ppm of soil phosphorous is associated with a 0.45 ppm increase in corn phosphorous (i.e., the estimated slope of our regression). Dr. Schneider additionally tests whether this estimated slope is greater than 1, which is a test for amplification of the phosphorous in the soil in the corn. This was done by looking at the confidence intervals for the regression slope. We had estimated the 95\(\%\) confidence interval for the regression slope as \([0.16, 0.76]\). This interval does not overlap with 0, which we can understand to mean that our analysis does not support that there is no effect of soil phosphorous. In addition, it does not overlap with 1, which we can interpret to mean that not all of the soil phosphorous can be converted to corn phosphorous. (Note that due to using the 9 observations we are getting some different numbers than Dr. Schneider’s notes). 15.4 Readings Either: Ch 6.1.1 to 6.1.6 of Quinn and Keough, or Ch 9.1 from Dr. Schneider’s notes.

The research question was whether Drug A (L-hyoscyamine) results in extra sleep relative to no drug, in 10 subjects. Cushny AR, Peebles AR (1905). The action of optical isomers. II. Hyoscines. J Physiology 32:501-510. The data are: require(dplyr) sleep.data = read.csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ahurford/biol-4605-data/refs/heads/main/data/extrasleep.csv")%>%filter(drug=="A") sleep.data ## drug extra.sleep person ## 1 A 0.7 1 ## 2 A -1.6 2 ## 3 A -0.2 3 ## 4 A -1.2 4 ## 5 A -0.1 5 ## 6 A 3.4 6 ## 7 A 3.7 7 ## 8 A 0.8 8 ## 9 A 0.0 9 ## 10 A 2.0 10 Note, that I loaded dplyr to filter the data because these data actually report extra sleep for drugs A and B, but this example from Dr. Schneider’s notes is only for Drug A. Note also that this is extra sleep which involves the mean value for the person’s normal sleep (no drug) being subtracted from the mean sleep when the person is taking drug A. As such, negative numbers mean that the person got less sleep, on average, when they were taking the drug. 16.2.1.1 Construct the model State our verbal hypothesis: People who take Drug A get more or less sleep. Graph the data: library(ggplot2) ggplot(sleep.data, aes(x = factor(drug), y = extra.sleep)) + # 1. Add the box plot layer geom_boxplot( outlier.shape = NA, # CRITICAL: Prevents duplicate plotting of outliers fill = "grey95", # Light fill to keep it as a background summary color = "maroon" # Muted border color ) + # 2. Add the strip plot (jittered points) layer geom_jitter( position = position_jitter(width = 0.2, height = 0), # Controls data spreading color = "black", # Pick a distinct color for raw data points size = 5, # Modify point size ) + labs( x = "Drug A", y = "Extra sleep (hours)", title = "Visualize the data (single sample t-test)" ) + theme_minimal()+ theme(axis.text.x = element_blank()) This plot shows that the median extra sleep is \(>0\), but not by a lot (small effect size) and also that there is a lot of variation between individuals such that the interquartile range overlaps with 0 (no extra sleep). There are also few observations. As part of our exploratory analysis we should also evaluate if the observations are symmetric around the median (i.e., to evaluate the assumption of normality). Formal model: \[ S = \beta_A + \epsilon \] where \(S\) is extra sleep (hours) and \(\beta_A\) (hours) is the mean extra sleep for the people who took drug A. This is different notation that Dr. Schneider’s notes, but I choose it to be more intuitive. The variable \(\epsilon\) denotes the errors and is \(N(0,\sigma^2)\). The null hypothesis is that \(\beta_A = 0\). 16.2.1.2 Execute the analysis Calculate the mean extra sleep. mean.extra = mean(sleep.data$extra.sleep) mean.extra ## [1] 0.75 (the data frame extra.sleep has 3 columns so I need to specify that I want to take the mean of the extra sleep column which is why $ is there. Alternatively, I could have used select() from dplyr). We have estimated \(\hat{\beta}=0.75\) hours. mod = t.test(sleep.data$extra.sleep, mu = 0, alternative = "two.sided", conf.level = 0.95) mod ## ## One Sample t-test ## ## data: sleep.data$extra.sleep ## t = 1.3257, df = 9, p-value = 0.2176 ## alternative hypothesis: true mean is not equal to 0 ## 95 percent confidence interval: ## -0.5297804 2.0297804 ## sample estimates: ## mean of x ## 0.75 The p-value and the 95\(\%\) confidence interval (overlapping 0) suggest that we cannot reject the null hypothesis that drug A does not change the amount of sleep a person gets. Dr. Schneider evaluates the model assumptions during this step, rather than exploratory analysis as presented in Quinn and Keough. This can be done with a qqplot. # Create the Q-Q plot ggplot(sleep.data, aes(sample = extra.sleep)) + stat_qq() + stat_qq_line(color = "red") + labs(title = "Normal Q-Q Plot", x = "Theoretical Quantiles (based on normal distribution)", y = "Sample Quantiles") + theme_minimal() This will work in place of Dr. Schneider’s plot of “Probability” versus “observations in rank order”. Many of the other assumptions of linear models are not applicable in this example of a one sample t-test. Independence of errors is pretty difficult to assess without more information on the study (the lagged residuals plot). We would like to partition the df and SS according to the model. Because we fit the model with t.test() rather than lm() we will need to calculate the SS ourselves. epsilon = (sleep.data$extra.sleep - mean(sleep.data$extra.sleep)) epsilon2 = epsilon^2 SS.res = sum(epsilon2) total = c("Total", "NA", sum(sleep.data$extra.sleep), round(sum(epsilon),6), SS.res) sleep.data2 = data.frame(sleep.data, epsilon = epsilon, epsilon2 = epsilon2) sleep.data2 = rbind(sleep.data2, total) sleep.data2 ## drug extra.sleep person epsilon epsilon2 ## 1 A 0.7 1 -0.05 0.0025 ## 2 A -1.6 2 -2.35 5.5225 ## 3 A -0.2 3 -0.95 0.9025 ## 4 A -1.2 4 -1.95 3.8025 ## 5 A -0.1 5 -0.85 0.7225 ## 6 A 3.4 6 2.65 7.0225 ## 7 A 3.7 7 2.95 8.7025 ## 8 A 0.8 8 0.05 0.0025 ## 9 A 0 9 -0.75 0.5625 ## 10 A 2 10 1.25 1.5625 ## 11 Total NA 7.5 0 28.805 SS.res ## [1] 28.805 SS total we can calculate relative to our null hypothesis that drug A does not change the mean number of hours slept. epsilon.total = sleep.data$extra.sleep - 0 epsilon.total.2 = epsilon.total^2 SS.total = sum(epsilon.total.2) SS.total ## [1] 34.43 The calculation of the p-value (0.21) from our t-statistic (1.33) needed to evaluate the df (stated as 9). Here the calculation to partition the df is shown: \[ \begin{array}{lllll} \mbox{GLM} & S & = & \beta_A & + \ \ \epsilon \\ \mbox{df} & 10 & = & 1 & + \ \ 9 \\ \mbox{SS} & 34.43 & = & 5.62 & + \ \ 28.81 \\ \end{array} \] The likelihood ratio is calculated as \(LR = (SS_{res}/SS_{total})^{-n/2} = (28.81/34.43)^{-10/2} = 2.4\). The observed difference (0.75 hours extra sleep) is only 2.4 times more likely than no extra sleep. This is inadequate evidence. 16.3 Report the biological conclusion The sample size is just 10 people. A power analysis suggests that we could have detected an increase of 1.29 hours slept. A bigger sample size would have helped us detect an effect. Our analysis did not suggest any change in sleep due to drug A. Additionally, given that the population is intended to be all people, it is unlikely that 10 people is a representative sample of the population. Extra sleep depends on drug. \[ S = \beta_{0} + \beta_{Drug}\mbox{Drug} + \epsilon, \] where \(S\) is extra sleep (hours), _0 is the grand mean of extra sleep (in hours; the grand mean is the mean withough considering drug type), and \(\beta_A\) is the amount of extra sleep for drug A relative to the grand mean (hours), \(\beta_B\) is the amount of extra sleep for drug B relative to the grand mean (hours), \(\mbox{Drug}\) is an indicator variable which is equal to 1 for the particular drug we are considering and 0 otherwise (unitless) and \(\epsilon\) is the residuals. For the notation \(\beta_{Drug}\), the values of \(Drug\) can be \(A\) or \(B\), which gives \(\beta_A\) and \(\beta_B\) as the possible values of \(\beta_{Drug}\). Our null hypothesis is that \(\beta_{A} = \beta_{B} = 0\) hours, which means that both drug A and drug B have the same effect. Our alternative hypothesis is that \(\beta_{A} \neq \beta_{B} \neq 0\) hours. 17.2 Execute the analysis Unlike the one sample t-test, where we had to use the function t.test(), when we have two-samples (i.e., groups or levels: the two drugs) we can use lm(), which is a function that we can use for all of our general linear models. sleepmodel2 = lm(extra.sleep~drug, data=sleep.data2) summary(sleepmodel2) ## ## Call: ## lm(formula = extra.sleep ~ drug, data = sleep.data2) ## ## Residuals: ## Min 1Q Median 3Q Max ## -2.430 -1.305 -0.580 1.455 3.170 ## ## Coefficients: ## Estimate Std. If there is any confusion about this, we should use the function as.factor() for us to tell the lm() function to treat the predictor variable as categorical (although here this is not necessary). Our results have been reported a bit differently than our model. We can make a QQ-plot evaluate the assumption of normality. We note that the original boxplot showed some right-skewedness for both drug A and Drug B. # Create the Q-Q plot ggplot(sleep.data2, aes(sample = extra.sleep)) + stat_qq() + stat_qq_line(color = "red") + labs(title = "Normal Q-Q Plot", x = "Theoretical Quantiles (based on normal distribution)", y = "Sample Quantiles") + theme_minimal() The deviation of the sample values from the theoretical values for large negative and positive values supports the right-skewedness of the distribution of the response variable. We can plot the distribution of our residuals for both of the groups: sleep.data2$residuals <- residuals(sleepmodel2) # 2. Plot using density instead of count ggplot(sleep.data2, aes(x = residuals)) + # after_stat(density) normalizes the bars so the curve fits the y-axis scale geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 15, fill = "steelblue", color = "white", alpha = 0.6) + # Layer a theoretical normal curve over the overall residuals data stat_function( fun = dnorm, args = list(mean = 0, sd = sd(sleep.data2$residuals)), color = "black", linewidth = 1 ) + geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "red", linewidth = 0.8) + labs( title = "Residual Histogram vs. Theoretical Normal Distribution", x = "Residuals", y = "Density" ) + theme_minimal() The plot above shows the residuals versus the predicted values against the normal distribution. There are too few observations to evaluate this assumption very well. The assumption of linearity does not apply to categorical variables. The assumption of independence is difficult to test without additional information. We should consider the bar plots (see earlier in this lecture) to assess the assumption of equal variance. Therefore, there are no large violations of the model assumptions. Dr. Schneider takes a resampling approach to test if deviations from the assumptions matter. We have not considered this yet, but this is an option if you wish to test whether violations in the general linear model assumptions affect your conclusions. You can see Dr. Schneider’s notes for details. 17.2.2 Partitioning SS and df The degrees of freedom for the model are the number of categories (i.e., levels or groups) - 1 = 2 - 1 = 1. \[ \begin{array}{lllll} \mbox{GLM} & S-\beta_0 & = & \beta_{Drug}\mbox{Drug} & + \ \ \epsilon \\ \mbox{df} & 20-1 & = & 2-1 & + \ \ 18 \\ \mbox{SS} & 77.37 & = & 12.48 & + \ \ 64.89 \\ \end{array} \] The SS values come from the anova() command and the formula: \(SS_{Total} = SS_{model}+SS_{residual}\). anova(sleepmodel2) ## Analysis of Variance Table ## ## Response: extra.sleep ## Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr(>F) ## drug 1 12.482 12.4820 3.4626 0.07919 . ## Residuals 18 64.886 3.6048 ## --- ## Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 The result of this F-test is that we fail to reject our null hypothesis that the mean amount of extra sleep is different for each drug given that \(\alpha = 0.05\) and \(p>\alpha\). This is fine, but perhaps you are wondering does drug B increase sleep? This is not the question we have asked or answered. We did have output to the question is \(\hat{\beta_0} + \hat{\beta}_B = 0\) earlier in the lecture. We found that the p-value associated with the mean amount of extra sleep for drug B (2.33 hours) was \(p=0.08\), while for drug A, this estimate was \(p=0.23\). While this value of \(p=0.08\) is close to \(\alpha = 0.05\), when we ask many additional questions, such as is \(\beta_0 + \beta_A = 0\) and is \(\beta_0 + \beta_B = 0\), we increase our type I error. If we ask 20 such questions, it is likely that one question will have a \(p<0.05\) just by random chance. Therefore, if we want to ask the question is \(\beta_0 + \beta_B = 0\), we need to consider a Bonferroni correction of \(\alpha/n\) where \(n\) is the number of comparisons we are planning (in this case \(n=2\), one for each of drug A and drug B). Therefore, when we test if \(\beta_0 + \beta_B = 0\) our threshold value for \(p\) is 0.025, and as such, we do not have support for drug B increasing hours of sleep. The proportion of the variance explained by the model is: SSmodel = anova(sleepmodel2)$`Sum Sq`[1] SSTotal = sum(anova(sleepmodel2)$`Sum Sq`) R2 = SSmodel/SSTotal R2 ## [1] 0.1613329 The likelihood ratio is: LR = (1-R2)^{-20/2} LR ## [1] 5.809031 This is not much variance in the response variable (extra sleep pooled by drugs) than explained by the model (grouping by drug A and B). An LR < 20 is considered insufficient evidence of a difference between the two means (drug A and drug B). 17.3 Report the scientific conclusion We find not support for the hypothesis that the effect of the drugs are different. There are only 10 people involved in this study and for both drugs there is large variation in how much extra sleep people get when taking the drugs. This study should have been conducted with more people, and stratefied to detect effects of sex and other physical and socio-economic determinents of health. This analysis could also have been done as a paired t-test (where we consider that the effect of drug A and drug B in a single person is related). We will consider this as a later date. 17.4 Readings Chapter 10.2

19 Fri Oct 23 (Quiz 3, A3 due) Randomization when assumptions are not met. 19.1 Last 20 minutes: Quiz 3 Dr. Schneider’s notes discuss using randomization when the assumptions of the linear model are not met. Below is the code to do this. I will illustrate this first with the corn phosphorous data (regression) and then I will illustrate it using sugar experiment data (one-way ANOVA). 19.2 Regression example corn.data <- read.csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ahurford/biol-4605-data/refs/heads/main/data/corn.csv") corn.data ## Psoil Pcorn ## 1 1 64 ## 2 4 71 ## 3 5 54 ## 4 9 81 ## 5 13 93 ## 6 11 76 ## 7 23 77 ## 8 23 95 ## 9 28 109 We can revisit the assumption checking that we did when did a regression for these data here. The exploratory analysis found that all our assumptions were quite well satisfied. Dr. Schneider performed a randomization for these data in Step 8 of Chapter 9.1 here. Dr. Schneider finds \(p=0.0079\) for 10,000 samples under random resampling, and concludes that the residuals not being normally distributed for this analysis does not change our conclusions. Our analysis of the data found that there was a relationship between the soil phosphorous and corn phosphorous. We will test the null hypothesis of no relationship by reshuffling the response variable data by randomly assigning response variable values (without replacement) to the explanatory variable values: i.e., if there is no relationship between the soil phosphorous and the corn phosphorous then it should not matter to which value of the predictor variable, we assign any of the response variable values. We will then re-calculate our slope coefficient given our re-sampled data, where we assumed the null hypothesis of no relationship between the explanatory variable and the response variable. We interpret the result of our randomization by evaluating the proportion of times that the randomized data (assuming the null hypothesis) resulted in an F-statistic larger then the F-statistic we calculated for the regression slope for the original data. In the original analysis, we calculated a p-value for that F-statistic by assuming independent normally distributed residuals with equal variance. For the randomization experiment, we equate the F-statistic with a p-value (describing the type I error) by calculating the proportion of times that the randomization experiment (assuming the null hypothesis) produced an F-statistic larger then the F-statistic calculated for the actual data. Psoil<-corn.data$Psoil # explanatory varaible # Make a function that calculates the F-statistic for the regression assuming the null hypothesis reg.func = function(){ resample.Pcorn = sample(corn.data$Pcorn,replace=FALSE) resample.corn = data.frame(Psoil=Psoil, Pcorn = resample.Pcorn) resample.mod = lm(Pcorn~Psoil, data = resample.corn) anova_result = anova(resample.mod) f.stat <- anova_result["F value"][1, 1] return(f.stat) } # repeat the reg.func() calcuation 10,000 times to generated 10,000 F-statistics assuming the null hypothesis random.f = replicate(10000,reg.func()) If you copy and paste this code into an R console (or script) run the function reg.func() a few times and observe that it calculates a different F-statistic for the randomized data, under the assumption of the null hypothesis being true, each time. The replicate function performs the reg.func() calculations 10,000 times. We can make an empirical cumulative density function of our resulting F-statistics: require(ggplot2) ecdf = data.frame(f.value = sort(random.f), quantile = seq(1,10000)/10000) g1 = ggplot(ecdf, aes(x = f.value, y = quantile)) + geom_line()+xlab("F-statistic values assuming null hypothesis")+ggtitle("Regression example: Soil phosphorous")+theme_classic() g1 Now we consider the F-statistic that we calculate for the actual data: mod = lm(Pcorn~Psoil, data = corn.data) # using the corn.data rather than the resampled data anova_result = anova(mod) f.data <- anova_result["F value"][1, 1] f.data ## [1] 12.8868 We calculate the quantile in the randomized F-statistic dataset for which our F-statistic calculated from the data occurs: ecdf = data.frame(f.value = sort(random.f), quantile = seq(1,10000)/10000) p.est = ecdf$quantile[min(which(ecdf$f.value>f.data))] 1-p.est ## [1] 0.0082 We estimate that 0.0086 of the randomly generated F-statistics (assuming the null hypothesis) are bigger than the F-statistic generated from the real data. 20 Mon Oct 26 - One-way ANOVA with random effects. This lecture is based on Chapter 10.4 of Dr. Schneider’s notes. We have mentioned random versus fixed effects a few times in class already. Today we will do an example of an analysis involving one explanatory variable that is a random effect. A Random factor categories that are considered a sample from some larger population of units, such as plots or fields in an agricultural experiment. A fixed factor has levels that are the only ones of interest, as in the analysis of sleep data in relation to drug. With a fixed factor we are inferring only to the levels at hand. With a random factor we assume that the levels are a sample from a larger population of levels or units, which vary. With a random factor we infer to a larger population of levels or units that might have been chosen. We often do not seek to test hypothesis involving explanatory variables that are random effects. Instead, we aim to quantify how much of the variation in the response variable is explained by the random effect. The choice between random and fixed depends on how we define the population. Example. A biologist carries out an experiment on the effects of nutrient enrichment on the growth of marine algae, at three different intertidal locations.Then repeats the experiment two more times, so that each location is exposed to each nutrient level on all three occasions. The nutrient factor is clearly fixed. The location factor is usually random. However, the location factor could be taken as fixed, if the biologist had chosen the locations to represent the fixed types of possible conditions in the study area (i.e., low, medium and high turbidity). The three occasions can also be taken as either random or fixed. They would be random if a known source of temporal variation, such as season and time of day, were selected at random. They become fixed if occasions where deliberated selected to differ with respect to a known source of temporal variation (i.e., sunrise, midday, sunset). 20.1 Tick widths on rabbit hosts: one explanatory varaible (rabbit), which is a random effect. Tick widths are measured on 4 different rabbits. Our question of interest is: Does the variance in width size among hosts (rabbits) exceed variance within hosts? Our formal model is: \[ W = \beta_0 + \beta_H H + \epsilon \] where \(W\) is the width of the ticks in mm, \(\beta_0\) is the grand mean of tick width (mm), \(\beta_H\) is the mean width of ticks on each rabbit host relatve to the grand mean (mm), \(H\) is an indicator variable corresponding to each of the four rabbits, and \(\epsilon\) are normally distributed errors. Dr. Schneider has a note that it is nice to use arabic letters, such as \(H\), for random effects and greek letters, such as \(\alpha\), for fixed effects. Let’s load and visualize the tick data: tick.data=read.csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ahurford/biol-4605-data/refs/heads/main/data/tick-width.csv") tick.data ## Wscut HostNumber Host ## 1 380 1 A ## 2 376 1 A ## 3 360 1 A ## 4 368 1 A ## 5 372 1 A ## 6 366 1 A ## 7 374 1 A ## 8 382 1 A ## 9 350 2 B ## 10 356 2 B ## 11 358 2 B ## 12 376 2 B ## 13 338 2 B ## 14 342 2 B ## 15 366 2 B ## 16 350 2 B ## 17 344 2 B ## 18 364 2 B ## 19 354 3 C ## 20 360 3 C ## 21 362 3 C ## 22 352 3 C ## 23 366 3 C ## 24 372 3 C ## 25 362 3 C ## 26 344 3 C ## 27 342 3 C ## 28 358 3 C ## 29 351 3 C ## 30 348 3 C ## 31 348 3 C ## 32 376 4 D ## 33 344 4 D ## 34 342 4 D ## 35 372 4 D ## 36 374 4 D ## 37 360 4 D The column “Host” (as a letter) ensures that R treats the rabbit identifier as categorical. Another option is to ask R to treat the host number column as.character(). In the above data, R is treating host number as an integer, and integers are numbers, so if we do not make it clear that HostNumber should be treated as a category, R might treat it as counts or ranks. I want the response variable (Wscut) to remain as an integer, so that we can have a numeric response variable. Here is a way we can do that: tick.data$HostNumber = as.character(tick.data$HostNumber) tick.data ## Wscut HostNumber Host ## 1 380 1 A ## 2 376 1 A ## 3 360 1 A ## 4 368 1 A ## 5 372 1 A ## 6 366 1 A ## 7 374 1 A ## 8 382 1 A ## 9 350 2 B ## 10 356 2 B ## 11 358 2 B ## 12 376 2 B ## 13 338 2 B ## 14 342 2 B ## 15 366 2 B ## 16 350 2 B ## 17 344 2 B ## 18 364 2 B ## 19 354 3 C ## 20 360 3 C ## 21 362 3 C ## 22 352 3 C ## 23 366 3 C ## 24 372 3 C ## 25 362 3 C ## 26 344 3 C ## 27 342 3 C ## 28 358 3 C ## 29 351 3 C ## 30 348 3 C ## 31 348 3 C ## 32 376 4 D ## 33 344 4 D ## 34 342 4 D ## 35 372 4 D ## 36 374 4 D ## 37 360 4 D The print out of the data shows that HostNumber is changed to a character, so that it will be treated as a category in the analysis. We also have the column Host, which we can always use to check that there has not been a mistake in treating HostNumber as a rank or integer. Let’s visualize the tick data: library(ggplot2) ggplot(tick.data, aes(x = factor(HostNumber), y = Wscut)) + # 1. Add the box plot layer geom_boxplot( outlier.shape = NA, # CRITICAL: Prevents duplicate plotting of outliers fill = c("maroon", "darkgray", "lightblue", "gold2"), color = c("maroon", "darkgray", "lightblue", "gold2"), # Memorial colours alpha = 0.5 # some transparency so we can still read the plot ) + # 2. Add the strip plot (jittered points) layer geom_jitter( position = position_jitter(width = 0.2, height = 0), # Controls data spreading color = "black", # Pick a distinct color for raw data points size = 3, # Modify point size ) + labs( x = "Rabbit host identifier", y = "Scutum width (mm)", title = "One explanatory variable that is a random effect" )+theme_minimal() Based on this plot, it looks like some of the variation in tick width is explained by which rabbit they are on, particularly as the widest ticks seems to be found of rabbit 1. We can inspect the normality of our residuals: tick.model = lm(Wscut~HostNumber, data = tick.data) # This treats HostNumber as a fixed effect (when we check our assumptions by plotting the residuals) tick.data$residuals <- residuals(tick.model) # Plot using density instead of count ggplot(tick.data, aes(x = residuals)) + # after_stat(density) normalizes the bars so the curve fits the y-axis scale geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 15, fill = "steelblue", color = "white", alpha = 0.6) + # Layer a theoretical normal curve over the overall residuals data stat_function( fun = dnorm, args = list(mean = 0, sd = sd(tick.data$residuals)), color = "black", linewidth = 1 ) + geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "red", linewidth = 0.8) + labs( title = "Residual Histogram vs. Theoretical Normal Distribution", x = "Residuals", y = "Density" ) + theme_minimal() It looks like the residuals are quite normally-distributed. 20.1.1 Execute the analysis To perform an analysis with random effects, we need to load a specific package lme4. You can do this using the install.package() command (or see the Quantitative training guide). require(lme4) # fit the random effects model mod = lmer(Wscut~1|HostNumber,data = tick.data) # view summary summary(mod) ## Linear mixed model fit by REML ['lmerMod'] ## Formula: Wscut ~ 1 | HostNumber ## Data: tick.data ## ## REML criterion at convergence: 281.4 ## ## Scaled residuals: ## Min 1Q Median 3Q Max ## -1.7904 -0.7518 0.0493 0.7972 1.9190 ## ## Random effects: ## Groups Name Variance Std.Dev. ## HostNumber (Intercept) 55.01 7.417 ## Residual 114.42 10.697 ## Number of obs: 37, groups: HostNumber, 4 ## ## Fixed effects: ## Estimate Std. Error t value ## (Intercept) 360.630 4.129 87.33 From this output we see that the variance explained by the host is 55.01 mm\(^2\) and the unexplained variance (in the residual) is 114.42 mm\(^2\). Therefore, as the only explanatory variable is the random effect associated with each rabbit, the variation between hosts is the residual variance. Therefore, we find that the variation between rabbits (114.42 mm\(^2\)) is greater than the variation within rabbits (55.01 mm\(^2\)) and that 55.01/(114.42 + 55.01) = 32.5\(\%\) of the variation is due to the ticks being associated with particular rabbits. 20.2 Last 10 mins: Correct any errors on Quiz 3 20.3 Readings Chapter 10.4 of Dr. Schneider’s notes.

21 Wed Oct 28 - Parameter estimation using maximum likelihood estimation 21.1 Assignment 4 Assignment 4 (link) is due on Friday Nov 6 on gradescope. I have also added links to Assignment 3 (in case it was difficult to find the generic recipe). Please submit Assignment 3 as soon as possible. We have mentioned previously in class that taking the logarithm of the response variable is not desirable and that maximum likelihood parameter estimation (MLE) is an alternative in these situations. For a model of exponential growth, i.e., such as the increase in the number of COVID-19 cases at the start of the outbreak, historically, the logarithm of the response variable for the model has been applied so that the relationship between the predictor variables and the response variables are linear. Specifically, the exponential growth model is, \[ N_t = N_0 e^{rt} \] where \(N_t\) (units: number) is the size of the population at time \(t\), \(N_0\) is the initial population size (units: number), \(r\) is the net reproduction number (units: days\(^{-1}\)) and \(t\) is time in days relative to a reference date (i.e., when the population size was \(N_0\)). Exponential growth is a good model for population biology when population sizes are small (and this includes populations of infected people, such as the application to infectious diseases). We can take the logarithm of both sizes of this non-linear model to make the relationship betwen the logarithm of the response variable and the predictor variables be linear. Specifically, \[\begin{equation} \begin{array}{ccc} \ln(N_t) & = & \ln(N_0) + \ln(e^{rt}), \\ \ln\left(\dfrac{N_t}{N_0}\right) &=& rt. \\ \end{array} \end{equation}\] Given this transformation, we choose \(\ln\left(\dfrac{N_t}{N_0}\right)\) as our response variable (where \(N_0\), the initial population size has a known value) and then if we forced the regression intercept to 0, the slope of the regression, with \(t\) as the explanatory variable, is \(r\). We could implement such a regression to estimate \(r\), the net reproduction number of the population, but in taking the logarithm of both sides we have changed our assumptions about the residuals being normally distributed. In doing this transformation, now the residuals around \(\ln\left(\dfrac{N_t}{N_0}\right)\) are normally distributed, and relative to a response variable of \(N_t\) our estimate of \(r\) might be inaccurate. To avoid transforming our response variable we can fit the non-linear model using maximum likelihood. 21.2 Write the model We wish to estimate the doubling time for SARS-CoV-2 for the model, \[ N_t = N_0 e^{rt}, \] where the doubling time is calculated as \(t_D = \ln(2)/r\). Therefore, to calculate the doubling time, we need to estimate \(r\) in the exponential growth model. Consider our data, which is the number of reported COVID-19 cases in Newfoundland and Labrador from February 5, 2021 to February 12, 2021. require(dplyr) # This code involves a bit of data cleaning, but at the end our data is printed. COVID.data = read.csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ahurford/NL-public-COVID-data/main/NL_prov_stats.csv") dates <- COVID.data$date_of_update COVID.data$date_of_update <- format(as.POSIXct(dates,format='%Y/%m/%d %H:%M:%S'),format='%Y/%m/%d') COVID.data = filter(COVID.data,date_of_update >= "2021/02/05")%>%filter(date_of_update <= "2021/02/12")%>%select(date_of_update, new_provincial_cases) date = seq(as.Date("2021/02/05"), as.Date("2021/02/12"), "days") COVID.data <- data.frame(COVID.data, date)%>%mutate(t = seq(1,8))%>%rename(cases=new_provincial_cases)%>%select(-date_of_update) COVID.data ## cases date t ## 1 1 2021-02-05 1 ## 2 3 2021-02-06 2 ## 3 1 2021-02-07 3 ## 4 11 2021-02-08 4 ## 5 30 2021-02-09 5 ## 6 53 2021-02-10 6 ## 7 100 2021-02-11 7 ## 8 50 2021-02-12 8 Let’s graph our COVID-19 data to inspect whether fitting an exponential growth model to these data is reasonable. require(ggplot2) g1=ggplot(COVID.data, aes(x = t, y = cases)) + geom_point()+xlab("Days since February 5, 2021")+ylab("New reported COVID-19 cases")+theme_classic()+ggtitle("Alpha variant oubreak in Newfoundland and Labrador") g1 There is quite a bit of error deviation from exponential, likely due to undetected cases and reporting delays. Nonetheless, we will complete our analysis as a starting point. We will also assume that \(N_0 = 1\). 21.3 Writing the likelihood function Likelihood. Given the data, how likely is a parameter in the model. Can be contrasted with probability, where if the parameters are known, we can calculate the probability of an outcome. The likelihood function is, \[ L(\theta | y_1, y_2, \dots, y_n) = \prod_{i=1}^n p(y_i, n(t_i, \theta|\theta)). \] and the log-likelihood is, \[\begin{equation} \begin{array}{lll} LL(\theta | y_1, y_2, \dots, y_n) & = & \log\left(\prod_{i=1}^n p(y_i, n(t_i, \theta|\theta))\right),\\ & = & \sum_{i=1}^n \log\left(p(y_i, n(t_i, \theta|\theta))\right), \end{array} \end{equation}\] where, \(y_1, y_2, \dots, y_n\): are the observations reported for the response variable. \(n(t_i, \theta)\) is the expected value of the response variable for the explanatory variable value that corresponds to observation \(i\), \(t_i\), and \(\theta\) is a parameter (or a vector of parameters) in the model. \(p(y_i, n(t_i,\theta)|\theta)\) is the probability of the observation \(y_i\) given the parameter choice of \(\theta\). \(L(\theta | y_1, y_2, \dots, y_n)\) is the likelihood of \(\theta\) given the data. To write the likelihood function we need to make an assumption about the distribution of our residuals. For this COVID-19 case data, the numbers are small, so we might choose the Poisson distribution. The Poisson distribution only has one parameter (the mean), so fitting this model involves one less complication than assuming normally distributed errors, where the normal distribution has both a mean and a variance parameter. Therefore, I will complete this example assuming a negative binomial distribution of errors; to account for the small values and to show an example of fitting two parameters. I am going to complete my model fitting using the mle2 function from the bbmle package. require(bbmle) ?mle2 Using this function requires me to create a function that returns the negative log-likelihood. This function depends on two parameters that I wish to estimate, \(r\) and the overdispersion parameter in the negative binomial, which is size. N0 <- 1 # fix N0 = 1 nLL = function(r,size){ nLLi=NULL #preallocation for(i in seq(1,length(COVID.data$t))){ t=COVID.data$t[i] Nt=COVID.data$cases[i] mu = N0*exp(r*t) # the model-predicted value for time, t. nLLi[i] = -log(dnbinom(Nt,mu = mu,size=size)) # this is the negative log-likelihood for the observation made at time t, given the model, for a particular choice of r, and the overdispersion. } nLL = sum(nLLi) } I can check my function supplying some values of r and size. test.val = nLL(r=1,size=2) test.val ## [1] 44.20782 21.4 Fit the model Before I fit the model, I would like to check my negative log-likelihood function some more. I can fix size and make a plot of the negative log-likelihood: r.vals = seq(0.1,2,0.1) nLL.out <- NULL #preallocation for(i in seq(1,length(r.vals))){ r = r.vals[i] nLL.out[i] = nLL(r,size=2) } nLL.out = data.frame(r=r.vals, nLL = nLL.out) nLL.out ## r nLL ## 1 0.1 166.46890 ## 2 0.2 101.91043 ## 3 0.3 62.15926 ## 4 0.4 40.68094 ## 5 0.5 30.98082 ## 6 0.6 28.31345 ## 7 0.7 29.69811 ## 8 0.8 33.39383 ## 9 0.9 38.41487 ## 10 1.0 44.20782 ## 11 1.1 50.46069 ## 12 1.2 56.99544 ## 13 1.3 63.70869 ## 14 1.4 70.53907 ## 15 1.5 77.44921 ## 16 1.6 84.41572 ## 17 1.7 91.42348 ## 18 1.8 98.46241 ## 19 1.9 105.52558 ## 20 2.0 112.60807 We can plot these results: gnLL=ggplot(nLL.out, aes(x = r, y = nLL)) + geom_line()+xlab("net reproduction number, r")+ylab("negative log-likelihood")+theme_classic()+ggtitle("Negative log-likelihood profile when size is fixed at 2") gnLL From this graph we can see that when the dispersion parameter in the negative binomial is fixed at 2, the negative log-likelihood is minimized for \(r \approx\) 0.6 days\(^{-1}\). This illustrates what were are aiming to do for the parameter estimation. When we estimate the parameters using mle2 we will need to supply guesses of the \((r,1/k)\) parameter values (where the size parameter is denoted \(1/k\)) that minimize the negative log-likelihood. Note that the likelihood is maximized for the same parameter values as the log-likelihood because the logarithm function is monotonic. Note also that the parameter that maximizes the log-likelihood, also minimizes the negative log-likelihood. Let’s use the mle2 function to estimate our \(r\) and \(1/k\) for this model. fit <- mle2( minuslogl = nLL, start = list(r = 0.6, size =2), # Initial parameter guesses ) summary(fit) ## Maximum likelihood estimation ## ## Call: ## mle2(minuslogl = nLL, start = list(r = 0.6, size = 2)) ## ## Coefficients: ## Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(z) ## r 0.60813 0.03745 16.2384 <2e-16 *** ## size 3.99971 2.63948 1.5153 0.1297 ## --- ## Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 ## ## -2 log L: 55.57756 confint(fit) ## 2.5 % 97.5 % ## r 0.5271991 0.7006337 ## size 0.9274826 13.1798957 There is some risk with maximum likelihood of failure to converge or convergence to a local minimum. Therefore we should plot our estimates and our 95\(\%\) confidence interval. r.est = 0.60813 r.lower = 0.5271991 r.upper = 0.7006337 fitted.values = data.frame(t = COVID.data$t, mean = N0*exp(r.est*COVID.data$t), lower = N0*exp(r.lower*COVID.data$t), upper = N0*exp(r.upper*COVID.data$t)) g2 = g1+geom_line(data = fitted.values, aes(x = t, y = mean))+geom_ribbon(data=fitted.values, aes(x=t,ymin = lower, ymax=upper,y=NULL), fill="grey", alpha=0.5) g2 This has added the fitted estimate of \(\hat{r} = 0.60813\) days\(^{-1}\) to compare with the data. The shaded region is the 95\(\%\) confidence interval. The original data are the first layer of the ggplot. To answer the question of what is the doubling time for COVID-19 cases in this situation, we use the formula \(t_D = \ln(2)/0.608 = 1.14\) days. This means that if this pattern of growth in COVID-19 cases continues, we expect the number of cases to double after a little more than one day. Our 95\(\%\) confidence interval for this estimate is: \([0.99,1.31]\) days. 21.5 Conclusion My hope is that this code might be useful for you if you want to fit nonlinear models or non-normal error distributions. The theory of maximum likelihood is explained in Burnham and Anderson, 2004. Burnham and Anderson (2004) also explains how to select between different models, i.e., for example, this exponential model and the Susceptible-Infected-Recovered model, for example.
